en: Preface to the *Sāmmitīya-śāstra*:
Alas! If one discusses the matter that transcends [the mundane], it is like sparks struck from a flint or a flash of lightning;

to attempt to directly accept it is already to become dull and stagnant, and as soon as one engages in thought, one falls into delusion and inversion. How much more so when one gallops through chapters and sentences, vying in debate?

Whether right or wrong, when viewed through the eye of true reality, there is nothing that is not mere conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*). Nevertheless, as the faculties of sentient beings are not uniform, the medicinal teachings of the Dharma are manifold.

Thus, the Tathāgata specifically expounded various sūtras for those of middling and inferior capacities. Later scholars, in their commentaries on these sūtras, engaged with various treatises (*śāstra*).

Once these treatises existed, debates surged like billowing waves and disputes over right and wrong arose like sharp blades. Although this is so, within the ground of ultimate reality (*bhūtakoṭi*), there is no...
To accept even a speck of dust is like entering the gate of creative transformation (*jianhua*) without abandoning a single dharma;

how much more so when those who are Buddhas and Patriarchs instead pursue the delusive and turn their backs on the Real? Which sage or worthy would not reject evil and follow the good? Thus it is said: "Right is right and wrong is wrong.
A person who lacks the mind for right and wrong is no person at all. In the past, I once read Master Sengzhao’s *Wubiqian* (The Non-Transmigration of Things).
The treatise, for the most part, establishes non-transiency by means of each thing abiding in its own position;
it subsequently clarifies that the nature of things abides in each [moment] through the presence or absence of things in their present and past states, such that they neither go nor come.

In sum, the phrasing and meaning are elegant and incisive, representing the subtle insight of Master Zhaoshī’s unique vision. However, it does not accord very well with the sūtras. Why is this? For as for the time of "ancient" and "present"...
There is the non-existence of things; there is the non-migrating nature. Yet, regarding that which is called "the nature of nature," who provides its framework and who presides over it?
If one does not know the nature of nature, how can one avoid being carried away by time and altered by things?
Furthermore, how can one harmonize the spirit with the objects themselves? Thus, those who frequently read his writings often admire their phrasing while failing to examine their underlying meaning.
Master Cheng of Kongyin was but a single cotton-clad monk from Yanshan; yet, born in an age a thousand years later, he met with Master Zhao as if across a thousand years.
Therefore, he composed the *Zhengliang lun* (Treatise on Correcting Errors) to effect such an examination.
Regarding that discourse, it employs various digressions and metaphors throughout, establishing the *Sūtra* as the Dharma-seal; thus, Master Zhao’s treatise is as clear as the sun and moon.

Is it not, then, like a precious gem of a foot in diameter or a luminous pearl of the night? In the past, the ancient masters were neither falling into nihilism nor clinging to existence; they were pervasive throughout their entire being.
A single word illuminated the essence of the school and has been celebrated for a thousand ages. How could one say that Master Tancheng was tongue-tied?
This is erroneous. For when it comes to the pursuit of principle, even Buddhas and patriarchs have no grounds for refusal.
In the past, if a non-Buddhist uttered a single heterodox word, they would be struck down and decapitated to atone for their transgression. Master Sengzhao was the very eye of humanity;

how could he have been willing to reject others from a thousand li away with such contemptuous sounds and expressions? You must surely be attempting to forcibly elevate your own writings while disparaging his.
It was not Master Zhao who severed [the bonds]. Judging by the general course of events, Master Zhao wielded the hands of a ball-thrower to dance the sword of Gongsun;
he was one who acted through the extraordinary. Master Cheng deployed the *maṇi* jewel amidst the ranks at Julu and held the seal of emptiness during the fierce battle at Red Cliff;
he was one who acted through the orthodox. Thus, without the discourse of Master Zhao, there would have been no way to give rise to Master Cheng.

This distinction cannot be made without Master Tǎng’s clarification to bring forth the profound depths of Master Zhào. It may be said that they complement one another, but it cannot be said that they contradict one another.
Therefore, all the renowned masters and veteran monks throughout the land have engaged in a cycle of response and song, striving to elucidate this great matter;
it is not a matter of giving rise to a mind of birth and extinction. Should there be even a hair’s breadth of self or personhood, then [it would be so].
It can sprout within the square inch of the heart. I fear that the "Mysterious Pearl" has not yet been touched by my hand; the sun is still high.
Written on the auspicious day of the middle month of winter in the Gengzi year of the Wanli era, by the Pure Land Layman Li Tianlin of Yan.

The Preface to the *Wubhiquan zhengliang lun* (Treatise on the Non-transmigration of Things as the Correct Measure) states that the *Prajñāpāramitā* says: "All dharmas have no marks of coming or going; they are without movement or transition.

Master Sengzhao took this as the basis for his *Wubhiquan lun* (Treatise on the Non-transmigration of Things), yet his interpretation of its meaning was simply that each thing abides in its own nature (*xingzhu*). Let us consider this for a moment.
The principle that phenomena have no coming or going is pervasive throughout all the holy teachings; it is, indeed, the profound mainstay of our Dharma.
Yet, can the discourse on the "abiding nature" truly encompass this? I harbor doubts about this myself. Thus, I have examined the words of the sages, but found no scriptural proof;
I have sought the correct principles, but found no logical consistency. Nevertheless, there may be some evidence for these words, though I have not yet [found it].
I have seen it. The principle may perhaps be explained, yet I have not fully mastered it. Is there anyone in the world capable of exhausting its depths?
I have once consulted the renowned scholars within the realm, and none failed to react with indignation and a flushed countenance, reproaching me for my ignorance.
As for those who sought to provide a rational explanation or cite scriptural evidence for it, I have yet to see such a person. Regarding that "abiding nature" (xingzhu)...
Is it not that the [mere] discussion of the fruit is not the intent of our Buddha? Or rather, does there exist a profound purport beyond the realm of conventional teachings (*nāmavāda*)?
Surely it cannot be known through the conceptual deliberations of the intellect. Nevertheless, while principle is inherently beyond words, words do not transcend principle.
That the holy teachings of the Tathāgata have provided a model for ten thousand generations, such that neither celestial Māras nor external paths can obstruct them, is due to—

It is merely because names and phrases have their place. If Confucius composed the *Spring and Autumn Annals*, life and death, bestowal and seizure, resided within a mere phrase or a single character; yet for a thousand years, no one has been able to alter them.

How much more so in this treatise, where every section concludes that all things abide in their own nature—how could it be said that the words are here while the meaning lies elsewhere? As the Sūtra says:
It is true that the non-retrogressive Bodhisattvas cannot fathom the Buddha’s wisdom.

I have often set forth my own lingering doubts and cited the authentic words of the Sage to occasionally reveal my Master Buddha’s fundamental principle of non-transmigration (*amṛta*), thereby correcting those doctrines.
Thus, this treatise is not intended to refute Master Zhaō; rather, it is intended to refute what the world takes to be right. As for Master Zhaō...
When the mind is empty and devoid of things, what gain or loss can there be for it regarding those [phenomena]?

If the world and future generations were to accept them based solely on such words, would it not be unacceptable that the profound meaning of the eternal reality (*dharmatā*) of the entire Great Canon would sink into mere talk of "things each abiding in their own nature"? Nevertheless, how can one be certain of what is currently...?

Is this its truly authentic fruit? Or is it not its truly authentic fruit? There will surely be those in future generations throughout the world who possess the adamantine eye to gaze upon that matter;
they shall turn their gaze back toward this treatise, beyond the reach of ordinary intellectual judgment.
This may provoke a smile. Written by the later disciple of Xianshou,
Kongyin Zhencheng, at the Lion’s Den on Mount Tai during the winter of the Wuzi year of the Great Ming Wanli era.
*Wubiquanlun*, Fascicle One.
Written by the Śramaṇa Zhēnchéng of the Lion’s Cave on Mount Wutai.

Initially, when Chéng first read Master Sengzhào’s *Wubiquan*, he could not understand it for a long time. It was only upon reading the *Zahua jiaochao* (Commentary on the Avataṃsaka Sūtra) that he beheld the National Teacher...
Consequently, he considered this to be a confused and syncretic teaching of the Hīnayāna, asserting that there is no doctrine of migrating from this region to another.

He then redoubled his study of the treatise and came to realize that Master Sengzhao’s doctrine of "non-migration" was correct in its fundamental principle but flawed in its reasoning; it possessed the core tenet yet lacked the supporting logic.

Upon examining his arguments regarding the "insentience of Prajñā" and the "namelessness of Nirvāṇa," he saw that they were unified in their single emptiness, wondrously harmonizing with the Ultimate Truth.
This [text] is generally in accord with the Sūtras; even if a sage were to arise again, he would not alter its words.
Yet, regarding the principle of "Non-Transmigration of Things," it errs. Alas! A thousand-li steed must inevitably stumble once;

the brilliance of great wisdom must inevitably have one point of obscurity—is it not so? As for those who claim their doctrine is similar, they do not seek stillness by releasing movement; they must...
"Seeking stillness within all movement. It is further said: "The rivers and streams rush forward in competition yet do not flow;
the whirlwind topples the mountains yet they remain eternally still," and so forth. This is precisely stillness within movement, and non-transmigration within transmigration.
Naming the school after this principle makes it resemble the *Sūtras*. As the *Prajñāpāramitā* states: "All dharmas come from nowhere, and when they depart, they go nowhere. The *Avataṃsaka* says:

"All phenomena are without arising; all phenomena are without cessation," and so forth. What is meant by "resembling" [the truth] is that their causes are not valid. Regarding the invalidity of the cause:

the *Sūtra* (Śrīmālā) takes the emptiness of the nature of all phenomena (*dharmatā-śūnyatā*) as non-transmigration, while Master Sengzhao takes each phenomenon abiding in its own nature (*pratisthita-svabhāva*) as non-transmigration.
As for "emptiness of nature," the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-sūtra* states: "The nature of form (*rūpa*) is itself empty; it is not that form is destroyed [to become empty]."
It is empty. Furthermore, it says: "The prior limit of form cannot be apprehended; its middle limit and its posterior limit are likewise both unapprehendable.
It further says: "Form is itself emptiness. This is the reason for non-transmigration. It also says: "This mark of the emptiness of all dharmas is neither arising nor ceasing," and so forth.

“Neither arising nor ceasing” is the principle of non-transmigration (*apravartana*). The *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* states: “The body, mind, and all sensory faculties are entirely empty and devoid of intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāva*);
this is the cause for non-transmigration. It further states: “By means of this continuous flow, there is nothing that can cause it to turn [into something else];
this is the principle of non-transmigration. That same scripture also asks: “How can one speak of the aggregates (*skandha*)? What is the nature of the aggregates? The nature of the aggregates—
It cannot be extinguished; therefore, it is said to be "unborn. That the aggregates (skandhas) are without birth or extinction is precisely what is meant by "the non-transmigration of things.

The subsequent verse sets forth the reason for this: "When these various aggregates are analyzed, their nature is fundamentally empty and quiescent. Because they are empty, they cannot be extinguished; this is the meaning of 'unborn.
All such statements mean that because the nature of things is empty, they do not transmigrate; it does not mean that there are actual entities that do not transmigrate.
Furthermore, as for what is called "abiding by nature" (*prakṛti-sthiti*), it refers to that which is said: "A thing of the past abides in the past and does not come to the present;

a thing of the present abides in the present and does not go to the past. This applies even to all things such as the new and the old, the young and the aged, arising and perishing, cause and effect, and so forth;

each abides in its own position and does not interact with others. All cases are like this. However, whatever has an abiding is termed "conditioned" (*saṃskṛta*); since it thus falls [into the category of the conditioned],...

That which is conditioned (*saṃskṛta*) belongs to the nature of arising and ceasing; it is not that there is no transformation. Therefore, the *Nirvāṇa-sūtra* (Chapter 30) states: "Abiding is called conditioned.

Since the Tathāgata has forever severed the marks of going, coming, and abiding, how can one speak of "abiding"? The *Mūlamadhyamakakārikā* states: "The goer does not abide; the non-goer does not abide.
Apart from the goer and the non-goer, where could abiding exist? The *Prajñāpāramitā* states: "One should have nothing to..."
"Abiding and yet giving rise to the mind. Non-abiding is precisely the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*).

Now, when the *Prajñāpāramitā* states that dharmas have no coming or going and no movement or change, it does not mean that dharmas have some place where they abide. For "abiding" is equivalent to "coming and going"; since there is neither coming nor going, how could there be abiding?
Master Sengzhao’s doctrine of non-transmigration is fundamentally based on the *Prajñāpāramitā* meaning of no coming or going; yet he [seems to] treat each thing as...
This is explained by means of the nature of abiding (*sthiti*). Now, does that nature of things actually abide? Or does it not abide?
There must certainly be a distinction between abiding and non-abiding. Therefore, Master Zhao set forth the reason why there is no transmigration:

"If one seeks the thing of the past in the past, it has never been absent in the past; if one demands the thing of the past in the present, it has never existed in the present. In the present... [it has never existed].
It has been observed that when one considers how things do not come from the future, they were already present in the past; thus, one knows that things do not go away.
Conversely, when seeking the present, the present likewise does not travel from elsewhere. This means that the thing of the past remains in its own past, not coming from the present to the past;

the thing of the present remains in its own present, not coming from the past to the present. The essential meaning of this entire treatise does not exceed this point, yet many people provide erroneous interpretations. Now...

To clarify Master Zhao’s intent, I maintain that the reason things do not undergo transmigration is that each thing abides in its own nature within a single world-period and does not move to or from another.
Why is this? If one seeks the object of yesterday in yesterday, it exists;
if one seeks the object of yesterday in today, it is absent. Therefore, we know that the object of the past abides in the past.

(If it did not abide in the past, it would not exist in the past; since it does not exist in the past, we know that the object of the past originally abided in the past. It does not come into the present. (If it were to come into the present, it would then exist in the present.)
Since it does not exist now, we know that the things of the past do not come into the present. Since the things of the past are thus, so too are the things of the present.
That is to say, if one seeks the things of today in today, they exist; if one seeks the things of today in the past, they do not exist.

Therefore, we know that the things of the present abide in the present and do not go back to the past (one should reflect on this by reversing the above). Thus it is said: "If one turns back and seeks the present, the present likewise does not [exist there]."
It is like seeking the Duke of Zhou when he was in Zhou: he was never absent from Zhou at that time.
Seeking the Duke of Zhou when he was in Jin: he was never present in Jin at that time. Thus we know that the Duke of Zhou resided in Zhou and did not come to Jin.
Seeking Yang Hu when he was in Jin: he was never absent from Jin at that time. Demanding Yang Hu when he was in Zhou: he was never present in Zhou at that time. Therefore...
One knows that Yang Hu remained in Jin and did not go to Zhou. It is like two boats traveling one after the other:
the front boat carries fish, and the rear boat carries bamboo shoots. Although the boats travel a thousand li, the fish and the bamboo shoots each remain in their respective boats and never move.

(If one seeks the fish of the front boat from the front boat, they are there; if one demands the fish of the front boat from the rear boat, they are not. The same applies to the rear boat: if one seeks the bamboo shoots of the rear boat [from the rear boat, they are there; if one demands them from the front boat, they are not]).

The bamboo shoots exist on the later boat; if one seeks the bamboo shoots of the later boat on the earlier boat, they are not there. If the fish of the earlier boat were present on the later boat, one could say that the objects of the earlier boat have moved over. Since there are no fish on the later boat, it cannot be said that the objects of the earlier boat have moved over.

If the bamboo shoots of the later boat were present on the earlier boat, one could say that the objects of the later boat have moved away. Since there are no bamboo shoots on the earlier boat, it cannot be said that the objects of the later boat have moved away.
The general meaning is simply this: things of the past abide in the past and do not come to the present; things of the present abide in the present and do not go to the past. This is [the principle].
This means that each entity abides in its own nature within a single moment; thus, it is established that there is no transmigration.
What is said—namely, that the new does not arrive at the old, nor does the old arrive at the new; youth does not become old age, nor does old age become youth;

the cause does not become the effect, nor does the effect become the cause, and so forth—is merely this point illustrated in a single treatise. If one examines it closely, what is said regarding the rivers competing to flow and...
The phrase "not flowing," and so forth, also carries this same meaning. That is to say: if one seeks the preceding wave in the preceding moment, it was never absent there;
if one demands the preceding wave in the subsequent moment, it was never present there. Because it was never present in the subsequent moment, it is clear that the wave does not come;

because it was never absent in the preceding moment, we know that the wave does not go. Since it is thus with the preceding wave, it is the same for the succeeding wave. This, then, is the case with the preceding thought-moment.

The wave of the preceding moment abides in that preceding moment and does not come to the succeeding moment; the wave of the succeeding moment abides in that succeeding moment and does not go back to the preceding moment.
Thus, while there is a continuous flow of waves from moment to moment, each moment abides in itself. Therefore, it is said that they "rush together yet do not flow.
This means that things each abide in their own nature within a single world-period, without coming or going. This is Master Sengzhao’s fundamental principle of non-transmigration.

If we now examine this against the sacred teachings, it appears not to be so. Why? Master Sengzhao, in seeking the nature of things, stated that "in the past they were never non-existent, and in the present they have never existed. This implies that these things existed in the past but do not exist now.

If a thing existed in the past but does not exist now, it is an impermanent phenomenon (*anitya-dharma*), not something that does not undergo transition. Therefore, the *Nirvāṇa-sūtra* (Chapter 20) says: "If, in the world..."
If a phenomenon (dharma) exists originally but is now absent, it is called impermanent (*anitya*). For example, things such as a vase do not exist originally but come into existence now;

having existed, they again cease to be, and are therefore called impermanent. Thus, [your claim that] what previously existed is now absent does not directly establish your thesis of non-transmigration;

on the contrary, it establishes the very thesis of transmigration and cessation that you seek to refute. As the *Mūlamadhyamakakārikā* states: "If a phenomenon has an intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) from the beginning, it is called permanent."
That which previously existed but now does not exist is what is called "annihilation. This implies that what was formerly present is now gone;
it is not the case that impermanence itself is annihilation. How, then, can this establish the principle of Prajñā as being non-transmigratory? Someone asked:

Master Zhaogong’s *Zongben* states, "To speak of 'neither existence nor non-existence' is not like the existence of those with views of existence or permanence, nor the non-existence of those with views of nihilism or annihilation. Now, [the text] says:
"What existed previously but does not exist now—is this not the existence of non-existence, the non-existence of non-non-existence? He replied: "Not so.

Master Zhao [Sengzhao] himself said that when one seeks the object of the 'previous' in the 'previous,' it was never non-existent in the 'previous'; yet when one demands the object of the 'previous' in the 'now,' it is never existent in the 'now.
This clearly means that the object of the 'previous' exists in the 'previous' because the conditions have not yet dispersed, and thus it is designated as 'existent. Now..."

Seeking for the object as it was before, one concludes it is non-existent because its conditions have already dispersed. Thus, what previously existed is taken to be existent, and what is now extinguished is taken to be non-existent.
To hold that what previously existed is existent is to grasp at existence as existence; to reckon that what is now extinguished is non-existent is to conceive of non-existence as non-existence.

To grasp at the conditioned as being existent is to fall into the view of eternalism; this is because one does not understand that the nature of dependent origination is fundamentally empty. To reckon the unconditioned as non-existent is to fall into the view of nihilism;

this is because one fails to recognize that dependent origination is devoid of intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāva*). As the *Mūlamadhyamakakārikā* states: "To insist on existence is to cling to eternalism;

to insist on non-existence is to cling to nihilism. Therefore, the wise should not cling to either existence or non-existence. Thus, although phenomena arise dependently and lack intrinsic nature, they are not... [non-existent].

Existence and non-existence are topics frequently discussed by Master Sengzhao. However, in his *Treatise on Non-transmigration*, he establishes the abiding of nature (*xing*), yet he nonetheless falls into this error;

this is truly lamentable. It appears he has mistakenly identified the "carrying away at night from the mountain ravine" of Zhuang Zhou as the view of Master Sengzhao, for it is not that the Master held such a conceptual attachment.

As the *Zongben* states: "Because existence is eternally empty by its very nature, it is called 'emptiness of nature' (*xingkong*). If this is so, then [the previous argument]— (Note: The provided source text ends abruptly. The translation reflects the available portion.)

When an object is present, and its conditions have not yet dispersed, is its nature not likewise eternally empty? If the nature of the present object is empty, one cannot say that it exists in the present.
Since it does not exist in the present, one cannot say that it is non-existent now. Thus we know that the abiding of the nature of emptiness is like the relationship between light and darkness;
they are diametrically opposed. As for what is said: "The object of the past remains in the past; the object of the present..."
Regarding the phrase "from now until today" and so forth: the fool says that since it is called "of the past," it is therefore something that has already ceased.

If a thing does not cease, it should remain eternally in the present and could not be called "past. Furthermore, a thing of the past abides in the past, and a thing of the present abides in the present;

these are distinct things in distinct times. Whatever consists of distinct things in distinct times is necessarily impermanent. Thus, the *Nirvāṇa-sūtra* extensively explains the practice of the sages.
To speak of impermanence through the distinction of phenomena is intended to refute the eternalism of the heterodox schools' attachment to "difference.

Now, to explain non-transmigration by means of different objects and different times contradicts both scripture and logic; therefore, it is groundless. Furthermore, time has no separate essence; it is provisionally established in dependence upon things.

Since things undergo flux and transformation, the names of the three periods of time—past, present, and future—are established based on the stages of arising, abiding, and ceasing. Yet now, your statement says: "The former object remains..."
In the past, that which now exists in the present is a conditioned phenomenon (*saṃskṛtadharma*) that falls within the categories of the past, future, and present.

Since it falls within the three periods of time, to claim that it does not undergo transition is impossible; such a thing has never existed. Thus, the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* (Chapter 20) states: "The eternally abiding dharma is not subsumed by the three periods of time.

The Tathāgata’s Dharma-body is not subsumed by the three periods of time, and for this reason it is called 'constant' (*nitya*). By contrast, this reveals that whatever is subsumed by the three periods of time is necessarily impermanent (*anitya*).

Who says that impermanence does not involve transition? Someone may say: "Master Sengzhao discusses non-transition (*bùqiān*) in terms of conventional phenomena, whereas the *Nirvāṇa-sūtra* explains the principle of permanence in terms of the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*).
Since these two do not correspond, it should not constitute a valid objection. I reply: The *Nirvāṇa-sūtra* states: "This body of mine now is precisely the permanent body (*nityakāya*).

This body is the transformation body (*nirmāṇakāya*); the permanent body is the true body (*sambhogakāya*). The transformation and the response-bodies (*nirmāṇakāya*) lack intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāva*).
The whole is itself the True. This, too, is to speak of the True while remaining within the conventional. Furthermore, Master Sengzhao states that "conventional things do not undergo transmigration.

Is it because these things are identical to the True that they do not transmigrate? Or is it because they are not identical to the True that they do not transmigrate? If they were not identical to the True, [they would transmigrate].

This refers precisely to conditioned, conventional things; they are not non-transient. If one were to claim that conditioned, conventional things are non-transient, this would merely be a deluded conceptualization based on emotional attachment. How could there be any conventional thing that is non-transient?

If one claims that conventional things are non-transient because they are identical to the ultimate truth, then both past and present things would lack intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*). Since they lack intrinsic nature, then...
Originally it was not born; now it is likewise not extinguished. Because it was not born originally, it exists yet does not exist, and thus one cannot say it previously existed.
Because it is not extinguished now, it is non-existent yet not non-existent, and thus one cannot say it is now non-existent.
Furthermore, since all phenomena are identical to Suchness (tathatā), that which is an entity is itself a non-entity, and that which is a non-entity is itself an entity. One entity is...
Many things are, in fact, one thing. The present thing is the past thing; the past thing is the present thing.
It is not that existence is extinguished to become non-existence, nor that non-existence arises to become existence; existence and non-existence share a single substance.

Nor is it that the one departs to become many, or that the many combine to become one; the one and the many are one reality. Nor is it that the present is pushed aside to enter the past, or that the past is displaced.
That which comes from the past arrives in the present; the present and the past are but a single thought-moment. This is what is meant by "the non-transmigration of things.
How could one allow for distinctions between the existence and non-existence of the present and the past?

Thus, even in a single speck of dust, nothing can be found to arise at its prior limit, and nothing can be found to perish at its subsequent limit. Its exterior reveals no surface, and its minuteness reveals no interior. It is like the Vajra King.
Being unmoving and indestructible, how could it be altered by coming and going, or by arising and ceasing? Therefore, the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states:
"The prior limit of form cannot be apprehended; its middle limit and its posterior limit likewise cannot be apprehended," and so forth.

If one perceives this principle, one cannot claim that a past thing exists independently in the past, or that a present thing exists independently in the present. Master Guo [Yuan] regarded this view as being confused with [the notion of] identity.
Regarding the Hīnayāna: since the Hīnayāna holds that conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta-dharma*) perish moment by moment, they do not migrate from this location to another.
This does not contradict the Mahāyāna doctrine of emptiness (*śūnyatā*). Master Sengzhao [held] that past things do not perish, and their nature remains fixed in the past.

To claim that there is no transmigration, however, contradicts the Mahāyāna doctrine of the emptiness of intrinsic nature (*svabhāva-śūnyatā*). (This means that if things were subject to arising and ceasing, they would lack intrinsic nature;

lacking intrinsic nature, they are empty. Thus, the *Nirvāṇa-rākṣasa-gāthā* says: "All conditioned phenomena are impermanent; they are dharmas of arising and ceasing. The Great Being of the Snow Mountains [Bodhidharma] sighed and said: "This is precisely the meaning of emptiness in the Mahāyāna. Master Sengzhao held that each thing abides in its own nature within a single lifetime without undergoing transformation, which implies the existence of fixed entities;
therefore, he contradicts the principle of emptiness). Thus his words say: "Therefore, the merit of the Tathāgata flows through ten thousand generations and yet remains eternally present. The Way..."

It remains steadfast throughout a hundred kalpas. A mountain is formed by relying on the first basket of earth; a long journey is reached by depending on the first step. This is because the fruits of one's deeds are indestructible.

Thus, although things belong to the past, they do not undergo transformation; because they do not transform, they do not transmigrate. Furthermore, it is said: "The fruit does not coexist with the cause;
rather, the fruit arises from the cause, and the fruit arises from the cause. Because the fruit arises from the cause, the cause does not perish in the past."
The fruit does not coexist with the cause; the cause does not come into the present. That it does not perish, does not arrive [anew], and does not transmigrate—this principle is clear.

I, the ignorant one, say that if past causes were neither to perish nor to transform, then sentient beings would forever lack the possibility of attaining Buddhahood, and the cultivation of causes would never have the prospect of obtaining their fruits.
Neither the Mahāyāna nor the Hīnayāna sūtras contain such a teaching. All the holy scriptures state:
The cause perishes and the fruit arises; only when the seed decays and rots does the fruit ripen. Therefore, the *Nirvāṇa-sūtra* (29) states: "It is like the sun about to set:
the shadows cast by mountains, hills, and mounds appear to move toward the east; it is logically impossible for them to travel westward. The karmic fruits of sentient beings are likewise so:
when this aggregate (*skandha*) ceases, that aggregate arises in succession, just as a lamp arises while darkness ceases, or as darkness arises when a lamp is extinguished. Furthermore, it is like...

When a wax seal is pressed into clay, the seal and the clay meet; the seal vanishes and the impression is formed. Yet this wax seal does not change and remain within the clay, nor does the impression emerge from the clay, nor does it come from elsewhere.
By means of the causal conditions of the seal, this impression arises. Thus, when the present aggregates (skandhas) cease, [the subsequent ones arise].
The aggregates of the intermediate state arise; the aggregates of the intermediate state cease; and the aggregates of the subsequent state arise—it is exactly like this.

Therefore, among the four conditions, there is the condition of immediate succession (*samanantara-pratyaya*). If the preceding thought-moment does not cease, the succeeding thought-moment will certainly not arise.

If one were to say that the Tathāgata did not transform [beings] due to past causes, then how could constant bodhisattvas ever attain the fruit of Buddhahood? By this, one knows that Master Sengzhao...

The doctrine that "past things do not transform" shares the same character as the common view. A questioner asks: "They say that because causes do not perish, one falls into the error of eternalism (*śāśvata*).
Now you say that causes perish; does this not lead to the error of nihilism (*uccheda*)? The answer is: "What we say here is that when the cause perishes, the fruit arises.

As the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi* states: 'Because the cause perishes, it is not eternal; because the fruit arises, it is not annihilated. Master Sengzhao accepts the arising of the fruit but does not accept the perishing of the cause."

Therefore, this falls into the view of eternalism (*śāśvata*). [The opponent argues: "From cause comes effect; we admit the arising of the effect. The cause does not perish in the past; we do not admit the destruction of the cause. Question:

"As it is said, 'A mountain is formed by relying on the first basket of earth,' and 'A long journey is reached by relying on the first step'—is this not precisely the case where the past cause does not perish, yet the accumulated causes produce the result?
Answer: This [notion] is the emergence of the eternalist calculations (*nitya-vāda*) of the non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*). Regarding *Nirvāṇa* (13), it transcends these externalist views of permanence.
[The opponent] says: "If the method of calculation proceeds from one to two to form hundreds and thousands, and if things were impermanent, then the 'one' at the beginning should perish.
If the 'one' perishes, who then reaches 'two,' and so on up to 'hundreds and thousands'? For this reason, all phenomena are permanent; it is exactly like this. [The Master replies:
This is precisely what the Tathāgata refuted by summarizing that there is nothing—whether distinct in form or distinct in mind—that is not impermanent. It has already been demolished.

It is so. I, the fool, maintain that the first step is not the last, and the last step is not the first. Since they are produced at different times and are distinct actions, they are impermanent phenomena;
they do not fail to change. Furthermore, if the first step were not subject to extinction, it would eternally remain at the beginning and never reach the second step, let alone travel a thousand li.

This can be understood by analogy with the accumulation of soil to form a wall: all such things are impermanent. How much more so regarding that which was sealed by the Buddha’s own golden mouth—how could there be any doubt? Question.

[Question: Master Zhaolun cites a scripture, saying: "The three calamities pervade all, yet karmic actions remain profound and still. Is it not the case that karma is eternal? [Answer: There are two meanings of "eternal":
first, unchanging eternity, which refers to the meaning of the non-transmigration of True Suchness (*tathatā*). As the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* says:
"Within the nature of true eternity, one seeks delusion and enlightenment, birth and death, coming and going, but finds nothing at all. Second, there is continuous eternity, which refers to karma.

This refers to what is called "the fruit not being lost. The *Avataṃsaka-sūtra* states: "While the self-characteristics of causes perish moment by moment, they gather sequentially so that the fruit is never lost.

A verse says: "One can fully comprehend both the perishing of causes and the gathering of fruits," because of the power of the perfuming of the equal and immediate conditions (*samanantara-pratyaya*) within the storehouse consciousness (*ālaya-vijñāna*).
When the preceding thought-moment ceases, it perfumes and gives rise to the succeeding thought-moment; thus, even though the kalpa-fire blazes forth, karma [remains].

The fruit is not lost; therefore, it is called "continuous permanence. Thus, although it is said to be serene, it nonetheless belongs to the category of conditioned phenomena subject to change and transformation.
Master Sengzhao’s attempt to use this to prove that True Suchness (tathatā) is non-transmigratory is, in meaning, erroneous. Question:
If causes perish, how can a virtuous cause yield a pleasant fruit, and an evil cause yield a painful fruit? Answer: The *Nirvāṇa-sūtra* says: "It is like a lamp..."
Although it perishes moment by moment, light destroys darkness; although food perishes moment by moment, it can satisfy hunger and bring satiety;
although medicine perishes moment by moment, it can cure illness; and although the radiance of the sun and moon perishes moment by moment, it can still cause plants and trees to grow.
Therefore, it is through the cessation of the cause that the fruit arises. Please observe the analogy of the wax seal; the principle becomes clear of itself.
This is called "illumination. It means that when the seal is high, its impression must be low; when the seal is low, its impression must be high.

Although the seal itself does not create the impression, the impression always corresponds to the seal without the slightest discrepancy. Yet it is only upon the cessation of the seal that the impression finally comes into being.
The causality of good and evil is exactly like this: the cause is able to permeate the effect; as the cause ceases, the effect arises. Although the cause...

The fruit does not arrive [from the cause]. By the power of perfuming (*vāsanā*), the fruit always resembles its cause; whether it be good or evil, suffering or pleasure, there is not even a hair’s breadth of discrepancy.
Furthermore, the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* says: "It is like a person who has consumed ambrosia (*amṛta*); although the ambrosia itself transforms, by its power, it can bring about immortality.
This is also the meaning here. Someone may ask: "If past things have already transformed, how is it that the events of the Buddha's previous births (*jātaka*) exist?"
"It can be spoken of. He replied, "It can be spoken of by means of names. It is like a person who sees various things in a dream;
upon waking, they are all empty. Although the dream-objects have ceased, they can still be described with clarity.

If one were to claim that dream-objects truly exist and remain in the past without transforming, that would be a foolish attachment. As the *Mūlamadhyamakakārikā* states: "If phenomena were to cease..."
Then it should not abide. If a phenomenon were not subject to extinction, such a thing would be impossible; how could there be a thing that abides in the past without undergoing transformation?
Even if one were to grant that a past cause does not transform in order to produce a present fruit, this too is impermanent and not something that does not change.
Therefore, the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* says: "The eternally abiding Dharma has neither cause nor fruit; space is eternal."

Therefore, there is no cause and effect. Generally speaking, whatever possesses cause and effect is something that can be produced; emptiness is not something that can be produced, and thus it has no cause and effect.
Master Sengzhao used the fact of being "producible" to prove non-transmigration; therefore, he contradicted the fundamental tenet [of the *Nirvāṇa-sūtra*]. Question:

Master Sengzhao clarifies non-transmigration by means of conventional phenomena, and thus [for him] there is cause and effect. The *Nirvāṇa-sūtra* reveals permanence by means of ultimate reality, and thus it excludes cause and effect.
The tenets and tendencies differ; one should not raise this as an objection. The answer is:

apart from the true nature of all phenomena (*dharmatā*), there is no principle within the Dharma of the Dharma-King that posits various causes and various fruits as being eternal. Thus, the *Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra* says:

"Mahāmati, false phenomena are eternal because their characteristics do not differ. It is not that false phenomena possess distinct characteristics; it is through conceptual discrimination that they appear so."
There is a distinction. Therefore, the essence of false phenomena is eternal. Thus, by means of the reason of non-difference, the thesis of eternal abiding is established.

The *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* also states: "Because all phenomena that are different are impermanent. What is called "different" means that at the time of the cause it is not the fruit, and at the time of the fruit it is not the cause.
At the time of the cause, since it is not the fruit, the fruit does not previously exist; at the time of the fruit, since it is not the cause, the cause [does not exist].
[The section on] "Later Cessation" states in the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*: "That which was originally non-existent now exists; having existed, it returns to non-existence.

Because this is impermanent, those who see no difference [between these states] realize the emptiness of nature (*dharmatā-śūnyatā*). Since the causal nature is empty and its essence is non-dual, how could this non-dual essence ever undergo transition?
Now, Master Zhao uses the fact that different causes produce different effects to prove non-transiency (*apravartana*). By doing so, he seeks to establish [the principle of] impermanence."

How could the doctrine of eternal abiding be attained? [Question: "If all dharmas have no coming or going according to the *Prajñā*, and *nirvāṇa* is eternally abiding and not a product of cause and effect, how are these points to be reconciled?

[Answer: "The *Prajñā* sweeps away marks to designate them as 'emptiness'; therefore it says that dharmas have no coming or going, meaning that when one seeks the marks of coming and going, they cannot be found. This does not mean it is manifesting eternity. *Nirvāṇa* directly reveals the true nature;

therefore it says it is eternally abiding and not a product of cause and effect. Thus the Sūtra says: 'The impermanent is saṃsāra; the permanent is Great *Nirvāṇa*. Emptiness is saṃsāra; non-emptiness is Great *Nirvāṇa*. This means that conditioned causes and effects are the dharmas of saṃsāra, and thus they are all impermanent. Impermanent dharmas possess no self-nature. To the very bottom..."

It is merely emptiness. Thus, impermanence is emptiness, and emptiness is impermanence. Since impermanence and emptiness are one and the same conditioned phenomenon (*saṃskṛta-dharma*), they both pertain to birth-and-death (*saṃsāra*) and are not *nirvāṇa* or the Buddha-nature (*buddhadhātu*). Consequently, *nirvāṇa* takes cause and effect as its impermanent aspect; this is precisely the meaning of the emptiness of all phenomena in Prajñāpāramitā.

That which is called "the emptiness of *nirvāṇa*" in the sense that the phenomena of Prajñā have no coming or going refers to birth-and-death. The eternally abiding and non-empty essence of *nirvāṇa* is the Tathāgatagarbha, the Buddha-nature, and the true self (*ātman*), which is firm, solid, and unchanging.

If it were not impermanent, it would not be truly existent; if it possessed a real essence, it would not be empty. This point has not yet been reached in the *Prajñāpāramitā Sūtras*. Those who are ignorant take the fact that the dharmas of *prajñā* have no coming or going to mean they are identical to the permanent, real nature of *nirvāṇa*; thus, both schools lose their respective positions.

It is said: People say that while the person remains the same in appearance, the body is one throughout a hundred years; they merely know that the years pass away, yet do not realize that the form follows along.
Thus, when a Brahmin who had left the household life returned with white hair, a neighbor saw him and asked, "Is that former man still here?"
The Brahmin said, "I am like the man of old; yet I am not the man of old. The neighbor was startled and did not understand his words.
The meaning of the Brahmin’s statement here is this: he meant that while the man of old was a youth, he is now white-haired; how, then, could he be called the man of old?
Therefore, the *Nirvāṇa-sūtra* says: "All phenomena perish first and arise later, continuing in a similar succession.
When ordinary people perceive this, they conceive of it as permanent; yet in truth, it is not permanent. Youth is the cause and white hair is the fruit.
Although the state of old age is obtained based on youth, it must wait for the youthful countenance to transform before the state of old age can manifest. If the vigor of youth did not transform..."

How could there be such a thing as a person with white hair? Since the youthful countenance has already transformed and the signs of old age have begun to arise, yet the cause and effect remain similar, it is said:
"I am the same person as before, yet I am not the person of before. This is precisely the meaning of the continuity of impermanence.

Master Sengzhao’s attempt to use this to prove the doctrine of non-transmigration is, in my estimation, erroneous. Nevertheless, regarding these three individuals—the Brahmin, the neighbor, and Master Sengzhao—within this context...
One should understand that scholars differ in their views. The Brahmin maintains: "The person of the past has already undergone transformation and does not come back now;

because conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛtadharma*) perish before and arise after in a continuous succession of similarity, one says, 'I am the same as the person of the past,' yet I am not that person of the past.

This indeed accords with the meaning of the correct principle of causes and conditions (*hetupratyaya*) in the Noble Teaching. The neighbor, however, maintains: "The person of the past neither perishes nor undergoes transformation."
It can be carried over to the present day; therefore, it is said that "the person of the past still exists. Master Zhao says: "The person of the past is neither extinguished nor transformed;
their nature remains in the past, but simply does not come to the present. The body of today originally abides in the present by itself and does not come from the past.

Both of these views are forms of eternalism (*śāśvata-dṛṣṭi*). However, because a neighbor [of this view] considers the substance of the present and the past to be one and the same as being eternal, [he claims] the past...

The body of the sun can reach this day. Master Sengzhao, however, maintains that the present and the past differ in substance, each abiding in its own world, and that immobility constitutes permanence.
This means that Master Sengzhao and his neighbor are both included among those refuted by the Brahmin. [The opponent] asks:
Is there anything in the world that has existed from of old without perishing or changing until this day? He replied, "There is. "What is it?
He said, "That which does not undergo momentary change (kṣaṇika) is it. "What things do not undergo momentary change?
He said, "Gold, diamond, the relics of the Buddha, space, and so forth. [The opponent] said, "Space is an unconditioned dharma (asaṃskṛta-dharma); it does not have moments."
It is so. It is true. The diamond *śarīra* is a conditioned phenomenon (*saṃskṛta-dharma*). Why would it not be momentary? [The answer is:

Because it is perceptible through direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), because there is sacred scripture (*āgama*) [to that effect], and because we directly observe that the nature of gold and silver remains unchanged and does not perish even after passing through thousands of millions of years.
The *Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra* says: "Furthermore, Mahāmati, just as gold, diamond, and the relics of the Buddha possess extraordinary qualities and are never destroyed, so it is, Mahāmati.
If there were moments (*kṣaṇa*) within the state of non-interruption (*nirantara*), then the noble ones would not be noble; yet the noble have never ceased to be noble.
Just as gold and diamond do not diminish even when weighed after passing through kalpas, why do the foolish and ignorant [not understand this]?"
[The Buddha] was skilled in my teaching of concealment. He conceived the notion of momentariness regarding all phenomena. The commentary states:

this clarifies that the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) realized by the Noble Ones (*ārya*) in the path of immediate succession (*ānantarya-mārga*) does not proceed by moments; it is not subject to arising and ceasing.

The example of the diamond-like *śarīra* (relics) of the Buddha is cited for this purpose. [An opponent] asks: Is there perhaps even a single thing in the world whose nature remains as it was in the past?
"Is it that which has ceased and does not come back? He replied, "There has never been such a thing. Why is this? All phenomena in the world fall into two categories:
those that undergo momentary change (*kṣaṇika*), wherein the preceding ceases and the succeeding arises, for it is impossible for the succeeding to arise without the preceding having ceased;
sentient beings and the like are of this category. Those that do not undergo momentary change are substances from former times that remain unchanged and unaltered until they reach later times."
The vajra and the Buddha’s relics are examples of this. How could there be a single phenomenon that abides in the past without perishing?
This is the view of worldly people: they believe that such things may exist. Master Sengzhao’s view is that, according to the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*), all things are non-existent.
Reflect upon this. Question: In the extensive teachings on *nirvāṇa* and the holy life (*brahmacarya*), it is stated that all things distinct from form and mind are impermanent. What of gold and...?

If the *Vajra* [Sūtra] and the Buddha’s relics already possess diverse forms, how could they not be impermanent? Furthermore, since these two sūtras contradict one another, how can they be reconciled?

I reply: Both are the words of the Sage, and it is truly difficult to reconcile them. According to my humble reflection, the *Laṅkāvatāra* comes first and possesses a provisional meaning (*sopadhiśeṣa-artha*), while the *Nirvāṇa* Sūtra follows later and possesses the ultimate meaning (*nirupadhiśeṣa-artha*).
It is like a later edict being able to annul a previous edict; how much more so in this case!

The precious jewels such as gold are formed from the waters at the end of an eon (*kalpa*); the relics of the Tathāgata are produced through the process of smelting and refinement. Since they were originally non-existent and now exist, they are impermanent.
Furthermore, because gold and vajra can be analyzed [into their constituent parts], they lack intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*).

The relics of the Tathāgata should exist in accordance with this world of humans and devas during an eon; when the eon ends and the realm becomes empty, it is logical that they should likewise perish. The Sūtra speaks of them in terms of their longevity.
At that time, it is "firmly abiding" (kṣaṇasthiti). This is because it is not of the nature of a moment (akṣaṇika), yet it is not ultimately indestructible.
Since the Tathāgata’s emanations have arising and ceasing, only the true unconditioned (asaṃskṛta) has a nature that is momentary;

its limit is not momentary, being firm, solid, eternally abiding, and ultimately indestructible. However, Master Zhaowei’s "Non-Transmigration" summarizes this by not departing from four reckonings, namely: existence... [text truncated]
There is neither identity nor difference. To seek the former object in the present is the view of existence (*astitva-vikalpa*), for that former object has never been absent from the present.

To demand the former object in the present is the view of non-existence (*nāstitva-vikalpa*), for it has never existed in the present. To hold that the former object remains as it was in the past and the present object remains as it is now is the view of difference (*anyatva-vikalpa*);
this is merely the omission of one [of the other] views. These four views are the great maladies of Prajñā; if even one of them is present, [the path is obstructed].

This runs contrary to the principle of Prajñā. How could it not be subject to change? What I, the fool, have long maintained is that Master Zhaowei’s doctrine of non-transmigration has a thesis but lacks a logical reason.
Someone asked: "I have observed that Master Sengzhao’s [treatises on] 'transience' and 'non-transience' never lean toward one side or stagnate in the other.
Why do you now specifically refute his 'non-transience'? The answer was: "Although he spoke of both, his underlying intent established non-transience alone.

Therefore, he used 'non-transience' as the title; non-transience is the primary subject of this treatise. As he said: 'To speak of permanence is to say it does not abide; to refer to departure is to say there is no transience. Though it is still..."
"Yet he constantly goes; though he goes, he is always still. These two statements meet in one realization; going and staying are of one essence.
He can be met through the spirit, but it is difficult to seek him through phenomena"—these are all similar expressions that cannot yet be used to judge right from wrong.
However, if we examine the context of his explanation, it simply means that each thing abides in its own nature within a single world, without coming or going.
There is no other explanation: although the world undergoes transition, each thing remains in its own original world and has never moved.
Viewed from the perspective of the world, things appear to move yet are always still; viewed from the perspective of the things themselves, the world appears to be still yet is always moving.
It is like a boat traveling a thousand li while an object does not leave the boat; the stillness of the object and the movement of the boat are two that are inseparable.
Therefore, their words say: "That which people call 'movement' is because past things do not reach the present;
that which I call 'stillness' is likewise because past things do not reach the present. What they mean is this:

people say past things do not arrive because they have shifted and passed away with the flow of time, like objects shifting as a boat moves; thus they say it is movement and not stillness. I, however, say that past things do not arrive.

Now, as for the original abiding of things in the past, it is like the original abiding of things in a boat; therefore, they are still and not moving. Both know that past things do not arrive at the present;
hence it is said that "what is created has never been different. They see things departing with the past, while I see things originally abiding in the past;
hence it is said that "what is seen has never been the same. In reality, what I call "abiding" is precisely what they call [the departure of things].
"Going"—what they call going is precisely what I call staying. In sum, although the three periods of time flow on, each thing abides within its own period without moving;
this is Master Sengzhao’s principle that movement and stillness are non-dual. But is the principle of the non-transmigration of my Prajñā truly like this?
If it were truly like this, then the Buddha would not have appeared in the world. Yet, Sengzhao...

Although Master Gong did not shift his position and cited the *Prajñāpāramitā* as the basis for his doctrine, his explanations of its underlying principles were all derived from the *Zhuangzi*, such as the passage on "carrying off a vessel through a mountain ravine at night";
thus, he ultimately remained within the realm of heterodoxy.

Question: Since that treatise is already in contradiction [with the truth], I request you to demonstrate the correct principle of non-transmigration. Answer: The meaning of non-transmigration pervades all the sacred teachings; its general purport has already been seen previously.
Now, I shall first present the essential summary and subsequently manifest the specific categories of meaning. As for the summary:

the ten directions and the entire dharma-realm are collectively one Great Perfectly Awakened Mind (*mahā-bodhicitta*). It is like a pure *maṇi* jewel, within which the myriad phenomena are densely arrayed.
Coming and going, arising and ceasing, appear as reflections therein. The deluded say that the pure maṇi-jewel truly possesses such characteristics of coming and going (transition).
The wise understand that these characteristics of coming and going are themselves the maṇi; in reality, there is not a single thing that comes or goes (it is non-transmigratory).
The wondrous, perfect, and awakened mind is likewise so. This applies to the holy and the ordinary, as well as the environment and its inhabitants.
Arising and ceasing, going and coming, appear as reflections therein. Those with ignorance claim that the pure, perfect *bodhi* truly possesses such characteristics of going and coming.
When observed with the eye of wisdom, these characteristics of going and coming are, in their very essence, quiescent; this is precisely *bodhi*.
In reality, there is not a single dharma that can come or go. It is like a person who, after a brief nap, dreams that a hundred years have passed;
during that time, the successive events from youth to old age appear with distinct clarity.

A deluded person does not understand this and claims that such phenomena of succession truly exist within the dream. The wise, however, clearly know that these are merely manifestations produced by the mind’s dreaming. Ultimately...

One does not take this to be real (that is, it is non-transmigratory). It is the same for sentient beings: due to ignorance, they falsely perceive the arising and ceasing, the coming and going, of all phenomena.
Viewed with the Buddha-eye, the true emptiness is darkly quiescent; in reality, there is not a single dharma that can come or go.
The *Avataṃsaka* says: "Inexpressible kalpas are but a mere moment; do not see length or brevity. This is the ultimate investigation.
This concludes the discussion on the nature of phenomena as momentary. Since phenomena have neither coming nor going, things do not transmigrate.

To explain this further, there are three perspectives based on the doctrinal gateways of the various holy teachings: first, the meaning of the impermanence of all phenomena; second, the meaning of eternal abiding and non-transmigration;
and third, the meaning of the unimpeded coexistence of both. Regarding the first point: all conditioned phenomena that arise dependently are impermanent. Momentary...
That transformation and change is not non-transmigration. Thus, the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* says: "The conduct of all ordinary beings inevitably and swiftly returns to extinction.
The *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* says: "All conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) are impermanent; they are dharmas of arising and ceasing. The *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* extensively explains that all dharmas are impermanent.
All these points share this same meaning. Regarding the second point, the meaning of "eternally abiding and non-transmigrating," there are two aspects herein.
First, it does not transmigrate because its nature is empty (*śūnyatā*). This refers to the aforementioned conditioned phenomena of arising and ceasing;

because they are produced by causes and conditions and lack intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), they are empty in their very essence. Since not even the slightest phenomenon arises and not the slightest phenomenon ceases, they do not transmigrate. As the *Prajñāpāramitā* says: "These..."

The Dharma has the characteristic of emptiness; it is neither arising nor ceasing, and so forth. The *Mūlamadhyamakakārikā* states: "All phenomena do not arise from themselves, nor do they arise from another;
they do not arise from both, nor without a cause. Therefore, it is said that they are unarisen. Unarisen means non-transmigration.
Second is true non-transmigration, which means that precisely because all phenomena lack self-nature (*svabhāva*), their entire substance is the eternally abiding true mind.
Like the Vajra King, it is immovable and indestructible; therefore, it does not transmigrate. The *Avataṃsaka* Sūtra says:

"Know that all phenomena are the self-nature of the mind. The *Śūraṅgama Samādhi Sūtra* says: "Within the true and eternal nature, one seeks in vain for delusion and enlightenment, birth and death, coming and going—nothing at all can be found.
The *Mahāyāna-śraddhotpāda Śāstra* says: "Therefore, all phenomena from the very beginning are free from the characteristics of verbal expression and free from the mind."
The characteristic of conditions is ultimately equal, without change or alteration, and indestructible; it is precisely this one mind, and is therefore called True Suchness (*tathatā*).
This is the meaning [of that term]. Regarding the meaning of "non-obstruction," there are two further senses herein:

namely, the non-obstruction between principle and phenomena (*li-shi wu-ai*), and the non-obstruction between phenomena and phenomena (*shi-shi wu-ai*). As for the non-obstruction between principle and phenomena, it refers to the aforementioned characteristics of movement and non-movement.

This is precisely non-obstruction. It means that because the unchanging principle is able to accord with conditions, the entirety of its nature—which is neither born nor extinguished—is universally present within all phenomena of birth and extinction.
It is like moisture pervading waves: thus it moves without moving. Therefore, the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* says: "The dharma-nature is fundamentally without birth;
it manifests as having birth. Furthermore, a sūtra states: "The Tathāgatagarbha and the seven consciousnesses..."
Both arising and ceasing are like a performer on stage. Furthermore, a sutra states: "The Dharma-body circulating through the five realms of existence is called a sentient being.
Moreover, because phenomena produced by conditions lack intrinsic nature, the very laws of arising and ceasing are themselves the principle of non-arising and non-ceasing;
it is like waves being identical to moisture—thus shifting yet not shifting. The *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* says: "Illusory falsehood is what is called 'characteristics'."

Its nature is truly the wondrously enlightened essence of clarity. The *Lotus Sūtra* says: "This Dharma abides in the station of Dharma; the characteristics of the world are eternally abiding. The *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* says:
"All dharmas are unborn; all dharmas are unceasing. These two are simultaneous; thus, there is no obstruction between change and non-change.
Second, regarding the non-obstruction of phenomena and phenomena (*śaśva-artha-vinirbhāga*), this means that all dharmas of the three periods of time are entirely true.
Because of the mind, whether it be time or matter, they are identical to the true mind. Its capacity for inclusion and pervasiveness is like that of a mirror or a lamp. Thus, a sutra says:
"In a single thought-moment, one universally enters immeasurable eons. It further says: "Without moving from the site of enlightenment, the body pervades the ten directions.
And it says: "The countless eons of the past are placed within the future and the present; the countless eons of the future are turned back and established in the past."
World! Thus, without moving a single speck of dust, one pervades the ten directions; without departing from a single kṣaṇa, one enters the three periods of time.
When one moves, all move; there is no movement, yet nothing that does not move. This is inconceivable by the intellect. The principles of movement and non-movement are fully exhausted herein.
These various meanings above—preceding causes and subsequent principles—are established through their mutual interdependence. That is to say:
Because all phenomena undergo momentary transformation, they lack intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*). Because they lack intrinsic nature, their entirety is the ultimate reality (*tattva*).

Because it is the ultimate reality, phenomena and principle are unimpeded. Because phenomena and principle are unimpeded, they are able to cause each phenomenon to accord with principle without obstruction.
These three thematic gateways pervade all the sacred teachings; none of them are not the discourse on the causes of transformation. Not...
"What does Master Zhao base his view upon? If there is no authoritative scriptural statement (āgama) to rely upon, then I, being ignorant, do not dare to accept his teaching.

Someone asked: "Master Zhao says that 'each thing abides in its own nature' (xingzhu). Is this not the same as the *Lotus Sūtra*’s teaching that 'the characteristics of the world are eternally abiding' (shichangzhu)? The answer was: "No.
What he means by 'abiding in its own nature' is that each thing abides in its own nature within a single temporal period (adhvan). That is to say, 'a thing of the past remains in the past.'"

Now, things exist in their own present state. It is like seeking a thing from its former state; that thing has never been absent from its former state, and for this reason, there is a thing abiding in the past.
The *Lotus Sūtra* says: "This Dharma abides in the station of Dharma; the characteristics of the world are eternally abiding.

The "station of Dharma" (*dharmasthiti*) is an alternative name for *tathatā* (suchness) [as Nāgārjuna explains in his commentary on the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra*: "The station of Dharma and the true aspect (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*) differ only in name"]. Suchness is the true reality of all phenomena.

Position: If one perceives all phenomena as having existence or non-existence, identity or difference, arising or ceasing, coming or going, these are all false conceptualizations and mental constructions;
they do not constitute seeing the true position of all phenomena. It is like a hungry ghost who sees the waters of the Ganges as a flowing fire;
such a person does not see the true position of the Ganges. (This metaphor is from the *Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra*). Just as there is actually no fire in that Ganges, so it is for the hungry ghost.
Beholding it, one perceives it as a flickering fire; its flames arise and cease in continuous succession, appearing and disappearing.

Yet the substance of that river Ganges remains ever as it was, never undergoing change. All phenomena are likewise: existence and non-existence, identity and difference, arising and ceasing, coming and going—none of these can be apprehended.
Nevertheless, sentient beings delusively perceive existence and non-existence, identity and difference, arising and ceasing, and coming and going; yet the Dharma abides in its own place.
How could it ever undergo change or variation? Therefore, it is said: "This Dharma abides in its dharma-position; the characteristics of the world are eternally constant.

If one were to say that this dharma existed previously but is now non-existent, one falls into the extremes of existence and non-existence. If one were to say that the present thing exists by itself in the present...

To say that "ancient things remain as they were in antiquity" is to fall into the extremes of identity or difference. There is nothing that exists or does not exist, nor anything that is identical or different, which is not subject to arising and ceasing, or coming and going.
Existence and non-existence, identity and difference, arising and ceasing, and coming and going are merely the pervasive conceptualizations of deluded imagination (*parikalpita*).

How could one possibly wish to align this with the principle of the True Aspect (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*) of the *Lotus Sūtra*? Yet, the reason why worldly phenomena are able to abide eternally is because they are devoid of...

It is simply because of their nature. That which is without nature in the world is precisely *tathatā* (suchness). Therefore, the characteristics of the world are themselves the characteristic of permanence. It is like a whirling firebrand:
its lack of nature is itself the Ganges River’s state of being without change. Thus, a sutra says: "The Buddhas, the Honored Ones with Two Feet, know that all phenomena are eternally without nature.
To say they are "eternally without nature" means that where there is permanence, there is non-existence [of inherent nature]. This is not a matter of logical deduction.
It is not that there was existence first and then non-existence; nor is it that this non-existence exists within that existence. It is like the flickering fire seen by those ghosts:
if one seeks the nature of this fire within the water, it cannot be found; yet if one seeks it apart from the water, it likewise cannot be found.
At the very moment the fire is seen, there is no fire to arise; and when it is not seen, there is likewise nothing to extinguish. Its nature is fundamentally thus.

They are non-existent by nature; it is not that they are made non-existent through some external force, nor that they were previously existent and later became non-existent, nor that this non-existence belongs to something else while that thing itself exists.
All dharmas are likewise so. That is to say, from the very beginning, they are neither self-originated nor produced by another, neither combined nor dispersed.

They are profoundly still and eternally quiescent; therefore, they are said to be "eternally without intrinsic nature. Because they lack intrinsic nature, each is individually true and spontaneous, and each is the true reality (*dharmatā*).

Being unmoving and indestructible, it attains eternal abiding. If one were to claim that this entity existed previously but does not exist now, then there would be "prior existence" followed by "subsequent non-existence.
Such a presence and absence constitutes annihilationism and violates the principle of the *Lotus Sūtra* regarding the absence of intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāva*).

Furthermore, because all phenomena lack intrinsic nature, they are all of a single nature (the absolute, non-relative One); this is called True Suchness (*tathatā*), which is without change or alteration.
It is indestructible; this is what is meant by "the characteristics of the world are eternally abiding.

If one were to claim that each thing’s nature abides within a single period of time without undergoing transformation, this would constitute a fixed dharma (*dharmatā*). A fixed dharma would necessarily possess an intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*).

Once there is an intrinsic nature, it contradicts True Suchness (*tathatā*). To claim that the characteristics of the world abide eternally while contradicting True Suchness is impossible. Furthermore, [as for] permanence...

The characteristic of abiding is itself the characteristic of quiescent extinction (*śānta-nirodha*). Thus, a sutra says: "All phenomena, from the very beginning, are eternally of the nature of quiescent extinction.
Since they are called "quiescent extinction," then regarding all phenomena, existence and non-existence, identity and difference, arising and ceasing, and coming and going are all unapprehendable.
Is it permissible to say that a thing of the past exists in the past and a thing of the present exists in the present? Or to say that what previously existed is now non-existent?
Is this not so? It is said that that which is eternally quiescent perishes as soon as it arises;

it does not wait for conditions to disperse before being called "perished. Thus, the *Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra* says: "That which arises at the very first moment is already subject to cessation; this is not taught for the sake of the ignorant.

Today, if one seeks the object of yesterday within yesterday, it was never absent there; thus, the arising of an object is taken to be its existence. If one demands the object of yesterday within today...

Now, that which has never yet existed is what is meant by the non-existence of a thing’s cessation. To regard arising as existence is called "definite existence," and to regard cessation as non-existence is called "annihilationist non-existence.
Yet you wish to equate this with the principle of eternal quiescence found in the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*; I do not know how this can be possible.
Nevertheless, the names "Dharma abides" and "Dharma occupies its station" are fully recorded in the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-sūtra*, and the Bodhisattva Nāgārjuna regarded them as true.

As for another interpretation, a master of divergent views in recent times has said: "The abiding of dharmas in their respective positions" means that the position of heaven is above and the position of earth is below;
the nature of water is inherently moist, and the nature of fire is inherently dry; the nature of sugarcane is sweet, and the nature of *huanglian* is bitter;

even down to the whiteness of the crane, the blackness of the crow, the yellowness of flowers, and the verdancy of bamboo—each dharma abides in its own position and cannot be altered or displaced. This is what is meant by...
"The characteristics of the world are eternally abiding. If one views it in this way, one merely perceives the distinct forms of individual objects as mutually exclusive;
one has only grasped the "characteristics of the world" (loka-lakṣaṇa), yet has not even dreamt of the "eternally abiding characteristic" (nitya-lakṣaṇa).

To claim that these things each abide in their own positions, fixed and immutable, is nothing but the deluded conceptualization of emotional attachment. This is contrary to the principle of the true reality (bhūta-tathatā) of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra*. It is... [contrary].
It is like a ghost who, failing to forget what it has seen, seeks the waters of the Ganges; this only serves to increase its burning heat.

Thus, the principle that "each thing abides in its own nature" is diametrically opposed to the eternal abiding of the *dharmatā* (real mark) in the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*. Yet, some consider them to be the same.
How could one not slander the *Lotus Sūtra*? Alas! It is not that I delight in disputation. What I loathe about purple is that it confuses the vermilion;
what I loathe about the counterfeit is that it confuses the genuine. Now, those who directly speak out in opposition are easy to understand;
those who use similar-sounding words to create confusion are difficult to discern. Therefore, the harm of direct slander is minor, whereas the harm of deceptive confusion is grave.
The harm is profound. How could I wish not to speak?

Having concluded the argument based on the authority of the sacred teachings (*āptavacana-pramāṇa*), if one were to further employ inference (*anumāna*), Master Sengzhao would set forth the reason for "non-transmigration" (*apravṛtti*) as follows:

If one seeks the object of the past within the past, it was never non-existent there; yet if one demands that same object within the present, it has never existed there. Thus, while it existed in the past, it is now absent;
this constitutes a contradiction of its own intrinsic characteristics (*sva-lakṣaṇa-virodha*), as the reason (*hetu*) functions upon a dissimilar instance (*vipakṣa*).

The formal inference (*pramāṇa*) is as follows: "The youth of the past is the subject (*dharmin*); 'it is necessarily subject to transition and cessation' is the thesis (*pakṣa*); the reason (*hetu*) is: 'it existed in the past but is now absent.'"
Therefore, it is a concordant example, just like the preceding aggregates (*skandha*). The preceding aggregates do not exist now; the preceding aggregates have already shifted and ceased.
Youth does not exist now; youth, too, has shifted and ceased. As for the claim that "the thing of the past exists in its own past and does not come from the present to the past," and so forth.

This also contradicts the reason (*hetu*). The formal argument (*pramāṇa*) is as follows: "The youth of former days" is the subject (*dharmin*). "It is not the case that it does not undergo transition and cessation" is the thesis (*pakṣa*).

The reason is: "Because it cannot be retained until the present. The concordant example (*sapakṣadṛṣṭānta*) is: "Like a dream from yesterday. A dream from yesterday does not reach the present; the dream from yesterday has already undergone transition and ceased.

The youth of former days does not reach the present; the youth of former days has already undergone transition and ceased. As for what is called "the past object does not transform": [this is refuted by the above].

This also contradicts the reason (*hetu*). The formal argument (*pramāṇa*) is as follows: "Past karma" is the subject (*dharmin*). "It is not that it does not undergo transformation and transition" is the thesis (*pakṣa*).

The reason is: "Because it is able to reach its result. The concordant example (*sapakṣadṛṣṭānta*) is: "Like yesterday. This means that if the cause were not subject to transformation, then the eternal cause would ultimately never reach its result;
