thus, this establishes that karma and its fruit are impermanent (*anitya*). Furthermore, the formal argument states: "Past karma" is the subject. It is determined...

The thesis is that [karma] reaches its fruit. The reason is stated: "Because the nature of karma is impermanent. This means that if karma did not reach its fruit, the nature of karma would have to be permanent;
thus, this establishes the fruit of karma through its impermanence. In this way, the two meanings of impermanence and the fruit of karma mutually support one another.

Who, then, could claim that the fruit of karma is permanent and does not transmigrate? However, Master Sengzhao’s assertion that past karma does not transform lacks any basis in the sacred teachings. There is...

The view of identity-and-difference. The formal argument (*pramāṇa*) is as follows: "The non-transformation of past karma" is the subject (*dharmin*). The thesis (*pakṣa*) is that it is erroneously conflated with the eternalist view (*śāśvatavāda*), while being held as a distinct [view].
The reason (*hetu*) is: "Because it contradicts both scripture and logic. The similar example (*sapakṣa*) is: "Like the contradiction with logic found in the nihilistic view (*ucchedavāda*).

For instance, it would be like an old man with white hair still possessing his youth, or a thousand-foot-long pine tree still possessing its original seed; such a principle is absolutely impossible. As for the contradiction with scripture: [text continues]
All the holy teachings state that the effect arises when the cause ceases. A question is asked: Since that [previous] explanation is contradictory, please demonstrate the correct principle.

First, the Dharma of Dependent Origination is demonstrated by means of a formal inference (*pramāṇa*). The thesis (*pakṣa*) is: All conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta-dharma*) are subject to impermanence and passing away.
The reason (*hetu*) is: Because they are produced by causes and conditions. The concordant example (*sapakṣa*) is: Like a lamp flame. A lamp flame arises from conditions; the lamp flame...
This is impermanent. Conditioned phenomena arise from causes and conditions; conditioned phenomena are impermanent. Regarding their non-transmigration, there are two meanings. First:

it is asserted that things produced by conditions are existent dharmas, and it is established as the thesis (*pakṣa*) that they definitely do not transmigrate. The reason (*hetu*) is: because they lack intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*).

The concordant example (*sapakṣadṛṣṭānta*) is: like a flower in the sky. A flower in the sky is non-existent, and a flower in the sky cannot transmigrate; such is the nature of that which arises from conditions.

It does not exist. Because it arises through conditions, it does not transmigrate; there is no substance here that can transmigrate. Second, it is said that an entity devoid of intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāva*) is a real phenomenon (*dharma*).

The thesis (*pakṣa*) is that it is definitively non-transmigrating. The reason (*hetu*) is: because its entire being is identical with the True [Suchness] (*tathatā*). The concordant example (*sādharmya-dṛṣṭānta*) is like a reflection in a mirror.

The substance of the mirror-image is the mirror itself; the mirror-image cannot be transmuted. The substance of that which arises through conditions is the True [Suchness]; that which arises through conditions is precisely non-transmutation.
This is true non-transmutation. These two are unimpeded. Furthermore, there are two meanings. First, it is said that "transmutation" and "non-transmutation" are existent phenomena (*dharmas*).
Their thesis is that their mutual identity is unimpeded. The reason is: in principle, there is no change, yet one follows conditions; in fact, [phenomena] are established.

Because the substance of characteristics is empty, it serves as a common analogy: like waves upon water. This is thus "non-transmigration while transmigrating" and "transmigration while non-transmigrating.

Second, it is said that "thought-moments, kalpas, lands, and atoms" are the subject (dharmin); "universal interpenetration" is the thesis (pakṣa); the reason (hetu) is "because all phenomena accord with the principle";
the common analogy is "like Indra’s net. Someone may ask: Master Sengzhao was a holy teacher; the doctrine of non-transmigration he established is [profound]. Why...
"Furthermore, for many years, whenever eminent masters and great craftsmen have composed treatises or established doctrines, they have invariably cited this as authoritative evidence;

I have never heard anyone dispute its validity. Who are you, then, that dares to recklessly scrutinize the insights of those who have awakened before us? He replied, "Alas! I, Tancheng, am but a monk of a single karmic consciousness.
How would I dare to debate with those who have awakened? I simply rely upon the words of our Buddha to establish what is correct."
If the words of our Buddha are indeed not to be contradicted, then even though Master Zhao was a sage, how could he be more sage than our Buddha?
As National Teacher Guanding said: "Always take faith in the Buddha; do not take faith in men. I follow this teaching.

Regarding the subsequent commentary on the "Discourse on the Non-Transmigration of Things," there are many who delight in making arguments; most of them are like those who try to prove that a tortoise is a turtle.

There is a master who uses the "Chapter on King Nimi" from the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* to comment: "Seeking the object of the past within the present; in the present, it has never been non-existent. His commentary states: "The child’s..."

"At that time, the skin and pores were moist and lustrous (formerly possessing youthful features). To demand those former things at this present time is impossible; they have never existed here now. The commentary states:

"In years of old age, the physical form is withered and haggard (now there are no youthful features). This evidence accords with the *Lunyu*, yet its meaning stands in opposition to Master Sengzhao. Why is this?
Master Sengzhao uses the fact that "what formerly existed is now non-existent" to establish the principle of non-transmigration (*bujian*). In the *Lengyan jing*, what formerly existed is now...
The unconditioned (asaṃskṛta) undergoes transformation; thus, while the cause remains the same, the manifestations differ. These two positions are diametrically opposed:

if Master Zhaolun is correct, the *Śūraṅgama-sūtra* must be incorrect; if the *Śūraṅgama-sūtra* is correct, Master Zhaolun must be incorrect. Among the teachers of men, none know how to distinguish between them—this is truly lamentable.
The case of *Nirvāṇa* is likewise [as previously cited]. Question: Furthermore, since the physical body already exhibits differences such as childhood and old age, or self and other, how can this be?
This establishes the reality of permanence. The answer is: if one perceives form as changing, it belongs to the realm of impermanence; if one perceives form as non-different, it is truly permanent.
That which is called the emptiness-nature of youthful countenance is non-different from the emptiness-nature of white hair; the cessation of Zhang San is non-different from the cessation of Li Si.
This statement of "non-difference" refers to non-difference in terms of identical substance (*tongti*), not non-difference in terms of similarity. All phenomena...
Because the nature of emptiness is non-dual in essence, this non-dual essence is precisely the true and eternal. Therefore, the *Prajñāpāramitā* states:
"The purity of form, up to the purity of the knowledge of all modes, is non-dual and not divided; it is without distinction and without interruption.
Thus, the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* extensively explains that things distinct [from the self] are impermanent, in order to refute the heterodox attachment to an eternal [self]. Indeed, the heterodox...
Having seen that the essence of nature is empty and non-dual, yet falsely claiming that distinct phenomena are eternally abiding—how could this be true eternity?

Thus, when Master Zhaor posits that "past things abide in the past and present things abide in the present" as non-transmigration, how does this compare to those who cling to the eternal abiding of distinct entities?
Is there a distinction between them, or is there none?

Question: How do we know that all distinct entities (*bhāva*) are impermanent? Answer: It is known by means of two types of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). First, the authority of scripture (*āptāgama-pramāṇa*):

because the noble teachings extensively explain that all distinct entities are impermanent. Second, the authority of reasoning (*yukti-pramāṇa*): for example, that which is non-distinct from space is called permanent;

whereas because conditioned forms and vessels are distinct, they are all impermanent. Regarding "distinction" in terms of duration: as it is now, it was not so in the past, nor will it be so in the future.
Things are not as they are now. Things of the past existed in the past but are non-existent today;
thus, these things first existed and subsequently ceased to exist. Things of the present exist today but were non-existent in the past;
thus, these things originally did not exist and now exist. Because they exist at one time and do not exist at another, they are impermanent. If...
Regarding the horizontal argument: it is as follows—that this thing is not that, and that thing is not this;

meaning that when one seeks this thing here, it exists, but when one seeks this thing there, it does not exist, and the same applies to that thing. It exists in some places and does not exist in others;
therefore, it is called impermanent.
The *Avataṃsaka* says: "For example, like the waters in a river, rushing and competing as they flow away, each unaware of the others;
so it is with all phenomena. It further says: "By means of this constant circulation, yet there is no one who causes it to circulate.
This bears a resemblance in its expressed meaning to Master Sengzhao’s four lines: "The rivers compete in their rush, yet they do not flow," and so forth. One seeks the reason for this...
If one establishes the cause [of this], then the two cases are vastly different. Why is this?

Because the *sūtra* teaches that all things are empty of intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) and lack substantiality, even though they undergo transmigration throughout the day, in reality not a single thing exists that transmigrates. It is like the water of a mirage; as it flows, there is no flow.
Therefore, the Sūtra first sets forth the cause, saying: "All phenomena are devoid of activity and also lack intrinsic nature. This is so.
Therefore, all of them are mutually unaware of one another. Later, the reason for this is stated: "The eye, ear, nose, tongue, and body are all empty and devoid of intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*).
Thus, because their nature is empty, they lack flowing clarity. Master Sengzhao takes the fact that each thing abides in its own nature as the basis for his doctrine of non-transmigration;
although the world flows constantly, each thing abides in its own nature within its own time, never having moved. It is as follows:
The boat in front carries fish; the boat behind carries bamboo shoots. Although the boats move along, the fish and the bamboo shoots each remain in their respective vessels and have never moved.
Therefore, it is said: "The present does not contain the past, so we know that things do not come; the past does not contain the present, so we know that things do not go.
Since phenomena each abide in their own nature within a single world-period, what substance could possibly come or go? This is the coarse [level of understanding].

Thus, each abides for a single moment. To observe this minutely, one finds that every thought-moment abides individually: the wave of the preceding thought abides within the preceding thought and does not come into the succeeding thought;
the succeeding thought is likewise so. This means that while thoughts flow constantly from moment to moment, each thought-moment abides individually.

Therefore it is said that they compete to pour forth yet do not flow [to the truth]. Since things already exist and each abides for a single lifetime without perishing or transforming, objects must possess a fixed nature (*niyata-svabhāva*).
If objects have a fixed nature, this stands in opposition to the principle of "no-nature" (*asvabhāva*);
how could this be merely a confusion of crimson and purple?
Question: Master Zhaol says that all things abide in their own nature; is this not the same as the meaning in the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* that "each does not know the other"? Answer:
When the sūtra says "each does not know the other," it means they do not touch one another and do not serve as conditions for one another.
This is truly because the essence and function of all dharmas are empty. Because their essence is empty, they are like images in a mirror: the beautiful and the ugly do not touch one another.
This is because, by virtue of being empty, they do not serve as conditions for one another—just as flowers in the sky do not produce fruit.
Thus, the cause does not become the effect, and the effect does not repay the cause; this is the meaning of their mutual non-cognition. Therefore it is said:
"All dharmas have no activity, nor do they possess an intrinsic nature. For this reason, all of them are mutually unaware of one another. Master Zhao says: "Because of causes and causes..."
The fruit exists; it is not non-existent. The cause does not perish in the past; it possesses intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*). Each phenomenon abides in its own nature; its substance is not empty.

Its efficacy flows on eternally; its function is not empty. The *Huayan chao* (Commentary on the Avataṃsaka Sūtra) classifies this as conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*), which it deems to be indistinguishable from the Lesser Vehicle (*Hīnayāna*).

However, because the Hīnayāna maintains that things perish in a single moment (*kṣaṇa*), what precedes does not reach what follows. Master Sengzhao [argues] that because the preceding thought does not perish, its nature abides in the prior state and does not arrive at the subsequent thought; how could this be the same as the Hīnayāna?
The Sūtra says: "The eyes, ears, nose, tongue, body, mind, and all the sense faculties—by means of these there is constant circulation, yet there is nothing that causes them to circulate.

By means of these there is constant circulation; they lack intrinsic nature and arise through conditions (*pratītyasamutpanna*). Thus, while not shifting, they shift; yet there is nothing that causes them to shift.

Arising through conditions, they lack intrinsic nature. Thus, while shifting, they do not shift. Master Sengzhao understood this. Why then would he [need to] say that "each thing [has its own nature]"?
If the nature of things abides in a single world-age without undergoing transformation, how could it not be immutable?

Some say: "Master Zhao [Sengzhao] held that each thing abides in its own nature; therefore, he took 'the absence of nature' as the nature. If this were truly the case—that the absence of nature constitutes the nature—then...
If that former object was originally non-existent within its own nature when it was present, then one cannot say it was "formerly existent.

If what was formerly existent is not actually existent, this is precisely existence being non-existence. Since it does not wait for conditions to disperse before it is called non-existent, one cannot say it is "now non-existent.
To seek that former object now and say, "it was existent in the past, but is non-existent in the present," is a form of attachment.
The conditioned exists, and the unconditioned is certainly non-existent; these are merely terms for the mundane and the ordinary. On what basis can one see that "non-nature" is itself "nature"?
If there were truly no nature, then non-nature would entail no arising; no arising entails no ceasing; and with no arising or ceasing, there would be no coming or going.

Since there is neither coming nor going, the principle of non-transmigration is clearly evident. Furthermore, why then should one stubbornly cling to the distinctions between the past and the present?

"Things of the past existed in the past; things of the present exist in the present. By fixating on existence and non-existence—claiming that what previously existed now no longer exists—do you not firmly invite the delusions of ten thousand generations? It is said:

"Among all things in the world, there is none that does not lack intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) and arise dependently (*pratītyasamutpanna*); how could it be that Master Zhao’s [Sengzhao’s] 'abiding nature' alone is not so? It is asked:
If this is so, then how could the divergent doctrines of the hundred schools and the dogmatic attachments of the ninety-six types of heterodoxies ever possess an intrinsic nature?
It is simply because we give rise to fixed notions where there is nothing to be grasped. How tragic!
The *Prajñā* says: "All phenomena have no characteristics of coming or going; they are without movement or transition. Their nature is like the water of a mirage:
it has neither the characteristic of flowing nor the characteristic of not flowing. To say that this water possesses the characteristic of flowing is an error."
If one claims that there is no characteristic of movement, that too is false. If one claims that this water remains with the preceding wave and remains with the succeeding wave,
such that they alternately exist and do not exist, is this not merely to insist upon the varying intensity of empty flowers or the actual length of a rabbit's horns?

Composed by the Śramaṇa Zhenceng of the Lion Cave on Mount Wutai.
Someone asked: "Master Zhao said that the reason Confucius gazed upon the river and Zhuang Zhou hid his mountain was because they were moved by the difficulty of retaining what has passed.
Was he not saying that one cannot push away the present in order to go toward the past? Is this truly the intention of Confucius and Zhuang Zhou? I replied: "No.
Master Zhao’s meaning was that things of the past remain as they are within the past; they cannot..."
They remain until this very day. Therefore it is said: "What has passed is difficult to retain. The things of today likewise exist only in today;
they cannot be pushed back into the past. Thus it is said: "How could one say that by pushing aside the present, one can move toward the past?
It is like the goods on a preceding boat which cannot be retained for a subsequent boat, and the goods on a subsequent boat which cannot be pushed forward onto a preceding boat.
This is called "the past thing remaining in the past and the present thing remaining in the present," with no mutual coming or going; this is termed "non-transmigration.
This [view] originates from the passage concerning "carrying away from the mountain ravine," yet it misses the meaning of Zhuang Zhou.
Zhuang Zhou said: "To hide a mountain in a marsh or a boat in a ravine is considered secure; yet at midnight, a person of great strength carries it away on their back. The one in the dark..."
One does not perceive this. This metaphor illustrates how the calculations of worldly people are extremely profound and subtle;

they believe their possessions will last forever without being lost, yet they do not realize that in secret, everything is shifted away by the forces of transformation (*zhao-hua*). In time, these things perish and cannot be retained. Therefore it is said:

"Whether hidden small or large, there is always something that escapes. To "escape" means to shift and perish. Master Sengzhao, however, considers this to be "non-transmigration"—how could this be so?
This is indeed the meaning of Zhuang Zhou. It continues by saying: "To hide the world within the world, one finds no place to escape.
Seeking this through our own school, it is as the ancients said: "The summit of the Tongxuan Peak is not of the human realm.

If one perceives this principle, then the characteristics of the world are themselves the characteristics of the eternal abiding. Therefore it is said: "This is called the great reality of constant things. *Heng* means "constant"; *qing* means "reality" (or "essence").
This is the reality of all phenomena, which is eternally constant and unchanging; thus, it cannot be subject to transition or extinction.
Therefore, it is said that "there is nowhere to which one may flee. Master Sengzhao—why not cite this as proof for the principle of non-transmigration?
Confucius stood by the river and sighed, saying: "That which passes away is like this [river]; it flows on without ceasing, day or night. "Passing away" (shì) means to shift, to go, or to be lost.
This sigh laments how the creative transformation of the cosmos flows on, ever-renewing and never halting; that which has passed is gone, while that which comes continues.
There has never been a single moment’s pause. This does not mean that past things abide in the past, nor that present things abide in the present.
Master Sengzhao said: "These are all cases where what has passed is difficult to retain; how could it be said that one must push away the present in order to go [to the past]?
His meaning was that past things abide of themselves in the past and cannot be retained until the present; present things abide of themselves in the present and cannot be pushed back toward the past.
Therefore, his words say: "That which was in the past remains in the past; that which is now remains in the now," and so forth.
Is the purport of Zhongni truly like this? Formerly, Zhongni once told Yanzi: "I have passed away on this very day."
"I have spent my entire life walking shoulder-to-shoulder with you, yet I have missed you; is this not to be lamented? You seem to be attached to that which I am attached to.
That [attachment] has already ceased to exist, yet you seek it as if it were still present—this is like seeking a horse in a deserted marketplace.
Now, Master Zhao says that past things abide in the past and present things abide in the present; is this not like seeking a horse in a deserted marketplace?
How lamentable! Formerly, Lord Jing of Qi shed tears upon Mount Niushan, saying, "How beautiful this state is! Why must these drops fall from this land before I die?
Yan Ying laughed at him, regarding him as an unvirtuous ruler, and said, "If you were to employ the worthy..."
If they had constantly maintained it, then Grand Duke Tai and Duke Huan would have constantly maintained it.

If they had caused the brave ones to constantly maintain it, then Duke Zhuang and Duke Ling would have constantly maintained it. If these several rulers had constantly maintained it, what would have become of the affairs of our lord today?
According to the words of Yanzi, this roughly resembles my teaching regarding the sequence of arising and ceasing within the four conditions (*pratyaya*).
(Also called "equal and immediate"). Yet Master Zhaogong stubbornly maintained that past things do not transform. Furthermore, he encountered the strange laughter of Yanzi. Master Zhaogong said:
"Since one speaks of 'ancient' and 'present,' why would one wish to shift them? My intention is this:

if it were possible to move the present into the past or change the past into the present, then one could say there is a shifting. Since the present cannot [be moved], how can there be any shifting? If this is so, then...

If that were so, then the present ought to remain eternally present, and the past ought to remain eternally past. Since this principle cannot be established, there is likewise no scriptural authority to support it.

Turning the case around, I ask: if you speak of "past" and "present" yet wish for them not to undergo transition, why is this? It means that the past is not fixed as past, for it was once called the present;
and the present is not fixed as present, for it will inevitably become the past. Thus, moment by moment there is flux and transformation, with never a single instance of abiding. Its...

Regarding the meaning of "non-transmigration": although past and present differ, they do not depart from a single thought-moment (*citta-kṣaṇa*). Since this thought-moment lacks intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), past and present are identical as one;
how, then, could there be transmigration? The *Avataṃsaka-sūtra* states: "Immeasurable and innumerable eons—when understood, they are but a single thought-moment.
Knowing that even this thought-moment is non-thought, thus one perceives the world. This is not a doctrine of abiding in a fixed nature.
The *Bujian lun* (Treatise on Non-transmigration) speaks only of each thing abiding in its own nature within a single lifetime. That is to say: "past things abide in the past;
present things abide in the present," and so forth. Thus, although a thing exists in the past, it does not transform; although a cause exists in the past, it does not perish.

Now, I interrogate him, saying: "According to the world, there are three [time periods]: past, present, and future. You claim that things do not transmigrate and merely abide through the present and the past;
yet you do not speak of the future. Why is this? He replies: "Things that have already arisen abide in the past;
things currently arising abide in the present. As for the future, they have not yet arisen. Since things have not yet arisen, they fundamentally do not exist. Therefore, I do not speak of them."

[The opponent claims: "There is a thing that abides in the future. [The proponent] challenges him: "If that were so, then since what has not yet arisen is fundamentally non-existent as a thing, how could there be a thing in that which has already ceased?
Since it is said to have 'already ceased,' how could there be a thing abiding in the past without having undergone transformation?"
If an object that has already ceased still persists in the past without transforming, then an object that has not yet arisen would likewise persist in the future without being deficient.
If an unarisen thing exists, how can it be called "unarisen"? If a ceased thing still exists, how can it be called "ceased"?
Furthermore, the arising of things occurs as a continuous succession of moment-to-moment arising and ceasing; it is during this very continuity that [the designation of time] is spoken.
This is called the "present," like a whirling firebrand. When a foolish child sees it, he takes it to be a real, stable form;

yet when a wise person observes it, even its momentary continuity cannot be found. Since there is not even a moment's duration in the present, how could one maintain that which has already passed as a fixed phenomenon, wishing for it to abide eternally without changing?
Among the Tathāgata’s immeasurable Dharma-gates, there is not one that does not prescribe medicine according to the illness.

Only the principle that all dharmas lack intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāva*) is like the Mahākacchaka medicine: there is no ailment it cannot cure. As the Sūtra says: "Form is itself emptiness," which means form lacks intrinsic nature;

"emptiness is itself form," which means emptiness lacks intrinsic nature. Because emptiness lacks intrinsic nature, emptiness is not [a fixed] emptiness; thus, the view of annihilationism (*ucchedadṛṣṭi*) is eliminated.

Because form has no intrinsic nature, form is not form; thus, one abandons the view of permanence. Furthermore, the present is not fixed as the present, for it will inevitably become the past; the present lacks intrinsic nature.
The past is not fixed as the past, for it was once the present; the past lacks intrinsic nature. This applies to all things—arising and ceasing, existence and non-existence.
Therefore, when one contemplates that all phenomena lack intrinsic nature, one finds that the world cannot be apprehended; thus, affliction [ceases].
The karma of the fetter of vexation arises without self-nature; thus one reaches the end of birth and death and encounters Nirvana.

This is precisely the benefit of discoursing on the absence of intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāva*). If you do not understand Master Sengzhao’s discourse that "each thing abides in its own nature" and his treatise on the "non-transformation of past things," what illness does he intend to cure, and what benefit does he achieve?

Someone asked: "The Indian scholars, when establishing or refuting a position, invariably take *hetuvidyā* (logic) as their standard. If the three members [of a syllogism] are deficient or erroneous, then what is established cannot be proven.

Now, Master Zhao did not move [from his seat]; what error or flaw was there that [Sengzhao] refuted him? He replied: [The text continues: "It is said: 'If the three members are deficient or erroneous, then what is established cannot be proven. Now, Master Zhao did not move; what error or flaw was there that he refuted? He replied: "..."
Master Sengzhao establishes that the past and present do not migrate. He says: "If one seeks the object of the past within the past, it has never been absent from the past;

yet if one demands that past object within the present, it has never existed in the present. This is the reason why the objects of the past do not migrate. Next, he cites this reason to establish his thesis:
"Because it has never existed in the present, we know that the object does not come; because it has never been absent from the past, we know that the object [does not go]."

It does not go. This is the thesis that "past things do not transmigrate. Present things are likewise so. Therefore it is said: "If one seeks the present by overturning [the past], the present also does not go.

Furthermore, if one were to establish the thesis that "past things do not transmigrate" based on the reason that "what existed previously is now absent," this would violate two types of fallacies according to the rules of *hetuvidyā* (logic):

namely, the "reason contradictory to the essential nature (*svabhāva*) of the property" and the "reason contradictory to a specific qualification (*viśeṣa*) of the property. Regarding the essential nature of the property...

The reason of contradiction with the intrinsic nature (*svabhāvaviruddha-hetu*) refers to the reason "that which previously existed now does not exist. Within the thesis of non-transmigration, this statement contradicts its own intrinsic nature;
that is, while "non-transmigration" implies permanence, "that which previously existed now does not exist" implies impermanence. Thus, it contradicts the intrinsic nature of the term "permanent.

The reason of contradiction with a specific property (*dharmaviśeṣaviruddha-hetu*) refers to the case where, according to the verbal expression, [the subject] previously existed but now does not exist.

This is precisely impermanence. If one infers Master Zhaò’s intention, he accepts that "that which existed before but is now absent" constitutes the persistence of intrinsic nature (*svabhāva-sthiti*).

This is because the entity previously persisted and neither perished nor transformed; it simply did not come into the present, and is therefore said to be "now absent. It does not mean that the former entity has already ceased to exist.
As for the contradiction regarding the distinct characteristics, this cause—"that which existed before but is now absent"—is capable of establishing everything intended by his position.
The thesis that "things abide, being neither destroyed in the past, nor coming from elsewhere, nor migrating" can likewise be established.

This contradicts the opposing thesis that "that which previously existed but now does not exist is impermanent, migrating, and subject to destruction. In this case, one also commits the fallacy of contradicting the sacred teachings (*āgama-viruddha*), because the sacred teachings state that whatever previously existed but now no longer exists is impermanent.
Furthermore, with respect to the fundamental thesis itself, it also constitutes a contradiction of one's own words (*svavacana-viruddha*).
The Preface states: "If one takes existence as existence, then one takes non-existence as non-existence. This refutes those who maintain eternal existence or nihilistic non-existence.
Furthermore, when establishing the thesis that "past things do not transmigrate," it says: "In the past, they were not non-existent; in the present, they have never existed.
Is this not precisely taking existence as existence and non-existence as non-existence?
Someone asked: "The Four Treatises were produced by a single person; why is it that only the *Buzhuan* (Non-Transformation) has obstructions?
If the *Buzhuan* has obstructions, how could the others not also have them? If the Three Treatises are free of obstruction, then the *Buzhuan* must also necessarily be free of obstruction. I replied:
"When people establish their words, unless they are Great Sages who have realized non-arising (*anutpāda*), they cannot be entirely pure and without flaw. Those who are brilliant and wise..."
Throughout my life, I have strived to ensure that every word I utter accords with reason;
yet, should I occasionally err, this is what the ancient masters meant when they said, "Before great wisdom, there is a fathom of darkness.

Nevertheless, can one say that because a single word was unwholesome, everything spoken throughout one's life was unwholesome? And can one, simply because various words were free from fault, [assume...]
Is it right to condemn a single word that was spoken in error? To condemn one's lifelong goodness because of a single erroneous word is inhumane;
to approve of a single erroneous word because of one's many good words is unwise.
Those who lack benevolence and wisdom are insufficient to discourse upon the Way. Therefore, to attempt to block the Three Treatises with the "unmoving" (bùqiān) obstruction is impossible.
Likewise, to attempt to penetrate the "unmoving" by means of the penetration of the Three Treatises is also impossible. Let us examine this:
the purport of the Three Treatises exhausts the profound and penetrates the subtle; it is the essential meaning of the Dharma-treasury and the vital core of the Sage’s teaching.

These are his words. As for the point that [the mind] does not migrate, there are certain discrepancies here that touch upon the fundamental principles and tenets of the Great Dharma; therefore, it cannot be left unaddressed.
Furthermore, Master Sengzhao was a hero among commentators. It is a pity that at that time, the Buddha-dharma had only recently arrived and its entirety had not yet been fully discerned.
At first, no one arose to challenge him with critical inquiry or debate, yet Master Sengzhao, possessing the talent of innate wisdom, proceeded to compose [his treatises].
This treatise, though containing occasional lapses, was not due to his lack of talent.
Had such a man appeared after the Tai and Liang dynasties, I would have known him to be a peerless figure in China; how could mere ordinary people possibly discuss him?
When Daorong criticized this work, some mocked him, saying that he was like a fool who dares to judge a sage. Daorong privately replied to them: "The reason I am able to [do so]..."
That I was able to meet Master Sengzhao was not due to myself, but rather because of the light of our Buddha’s holy teaching.
Had I not heard the holy teaching, I would certainly have regarded the doctrine of abiding in one's nature as the ultimate truth.
In a letter to Master Huanyou, the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* states:
"The Tathāgata also speaks of permanence, bliss, self, and purity; the world also speaks of permanence, bliss, self, and purity.
While the names 'permanence, bliss, self, and purity' are the same, that which constitutes permanence, bliss, self, and purity is different. How could these be conflated?"
How singular is this contemplation! Now, Master Zhao’s doctrine of seeking stillness through movement is similar to the *Sūtras*.

Yet, when one examines the underlying intent of his "immovability," it differs greatly from theirs. Why is this? The *Sūtras* take the emptiness of the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) of all phenomena as immovability;
Master Zhao takes the fact that each thing abides in its own nature as immovability. As for the meaning of the emptiness of intrinsic nature, it arises from...
Because form is emptiness, there is motion yet constant stillness; because emptiness is form, there is stillness yet constant motion.

This is the intended meaning of all the Prajñāpāramitā sūtras. Regarding the meaning of "abiding in nature" (*xingzhu*): it refers to what is called "that which existed in the past abides in its own past, and that which exists now abides in its own now.
Thus, although things exist in the past, they do not undergo transformation; although causes exist in the past, they do not perish, and so forth. To not understand this—
From which sacred teaching does this [position] derive? When one examines the statement that "movement is itself stillness," it appears that both sides are identical.

Yet, the emptiness of nature (*prakṛti-śūnyatā*) and the abiding of nature (*prakṛti-sthiti*) are diametrically opposed. Worldly people, seeing only a superficial similarity in a single phrase, conclude that they must be the same.

Failing to examine the underlying intent behind the establishment [of these views], you have instead conflated them into a single path, such that the distinction between crimson and purple can no longer be discerned.
If you, seated below, truly intend to champion Master Zhaosong, you must certainly be able to provide citations and demonstrate the reasoning for his position.
Only when this is done without contradicting the sacred teachings will my humble refutations be rendered self-defeating without further words. Since you are currently unable to do so—
To provide scriptural evidence for their reasoning, they stubbornly insist that this is so; who indeed could possibly agree with them?
Furthermore, regarding your letter’s citation of the *Avataṃsaka* and *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* sūtras to prove that "past things do not transform":
the *Avataṃsaka* speaks of Vairocana’s body abiding throughout the three periods of time, and the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* mentions the lamps of wisdom, the Victorious One, and others—all of these...
Regarding the evidence that past things do not undergo transformation, I, the fool, maintain that this proof is inconclusive. Why is this?

If the true body of Vairocana pervades every place throughout the ten directions and the three periods of time without any gap—so dense that not even a hair could fit between them—it is not like Master Zhao’s [Zhu Daosheng’s] view that something previously existing now ceases to be.
As for those such as Dīpaṃkara, although their traces of transformation have vanished, it does not preclude their being spoken of; as the "Chapter on Dīpaṃkara" states: "He..."
After the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, it is like a fire extinguished when the fuel is exhausted. The "Chapter on the Supremacy of Wisdom" states:
"Since that Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, such immeasurable kalpas have passed. How could one say that there is some entity residing in the past that does not perish?

If we speak in terms of the *dharmakāya*, then from the beginning it was originally unarisen, and now it is fundamentally imperishable. Your letter states: "If it is empty, it does not transmigrate; everything is annihilated."

[It is] extinguished. To further explain what it means for something to be "non-transmigratory," it is simply because one has not yet understood that form (*rūpa*) and emptiness (*śūnyatā*) are a single reality.
Although form and emptiness are non-dual, it is only when one sees that form is itself emptiness that one may say it is "non-transmigratory. As the Sūtra says:

"To contemplate all phenomena as empty and without movement or change"—how could this mean that there is some entity that does not transmigrate? If one were to take the existence of an entity to be "non-transmigratory," it would be very much like...
To cut down the flowers in the sky yet not discard them, and to cling firmly to dream-objects so that they remain for long—is this not ignorance?

In response: The Venerable Jie has come to say that one seeks past objects within the present; that within the present, they have never been non-existent. This is precisely what Master Zhao [Sengzhao] refuted when he dismantled the "non-existence" held by worldly people.
"Seeing" refers to people of the time seeking a thing in its direction and finding it non-existent therein; this is the non-existence of wrong view and nihilism.

Master Zhao refutes this by stating, "In its direction, it has never been non-existent," thereby refuting that [alleged] non-existence. Yet, if one examines this closely, it turns out that worldly people are actually refuting Master Zhao.
Why is this? For Master Zhao himself says that when one seeks a thing in its direction, it has never been non-existent in that direction.
If one attributes existence to things in the past, they have never existed in the present. This clearly takes what previously existed as being existent and what has now ceased as being non-existent.
To take what previously existed as existent is to cling to existence as existence; to take what has now ceased as non-existent is to cling to non-existence as non-existence.

To cling to existence as being existent is eternalism; to cling to non-existence as being non-existent is nihilism. As for the claim that worldly people consider a thing to be non-existent when it was previously present:
this implies that worldly people actually know that what was previously present is now non-existent, yet they do not know that what has now ceased is not non-existent.
That which was previously present and is now non-existent is "existence becoming non-existence"; that which has now ceased and is not non-existent is "non-existence becoming existence."
To say that it exists while being non-existent means that existence is not [true] existence; this directly refutes the prior view that things exist as substantial entities.
To say that it is non-existent while existing means that non-existence is not [absolute] non-existence; this directly refutes the current view that extinction is a nihilistic nothingness.
This is why [the argument] turns back to refute the worldly people who were attacking Master Zhao. Moreover, how could the worldly people ever hold such a view? It is simply you, sir, who—
This is a mistaken interpretation. That something existed previously but no longer exists now, or that what existed previously has perished in the present, is the common sentiment of worldly people;

yet Master Sengzhao also states that "what existed previously does not exist now. In this regard, what he has produced is no different from the common view. However, worldly people say that a thing from the past was "existent" while it was in the past;
now, when one seeks that thing from the past, that thing has already perished, and thus they say it is "non-existent" now. As for Master Sengzhao’s statement regarding things from the past...

They originally existed in the past, but they do not come into being in the present; therefore, it is said that they "do not exist now. This does not mean that the things of the past have already perished.
This is simply because what is perceived has never been the same: when worldly people perceive the impermanence of things, they say that what existed in the past no longer exists now;

whereas Master Sengzhao perceives that things abide eternally, and thus says that the things of the past remain in the past and do not undergo transformation. As for "coming," it refers to the initial basket of earth [of a tower].
The extinction of the mountain is also not established. The initial basket of earth does not extinguish the mountain, nor is its extinction established.
If this is so, do you, O Venerable One, desire its extinction or its non-extinction? Both extinction and non-extinction are unestablished; they are views of annihilationism (*uccheda-dṛṣṭi*).

To say "both extinguished and not extinguished," or "neither extinguished nor not extinguished," is merely contradictory conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*). Furthermore, Master Zhao himself explains: "Therefore, things..."
Although [the cause] existed in the past, it does not undergo transformation. Furthermore, you say that because the causal cause exists, the resultant cause does not perish in the past;
yet, you claim that both "perishing" and "not perishing" are untenable. Is this not for you, sir, to be undermining Master Zhao yourself?
Furthermore,

in response to the claim that worldly people give rise to the view of non-existence (*nāstika-dṛṣṭi*) because they seek after things that no longer exist— just as one might seek Zhang San from last year,

only to find that Zhang San has already died and thus conceive the view of his non-existence— it is argued that to grasp at non-existence as being "non-existent" is itself a false view (*mithyādṛṣṭi*) and constitutes a form of nihilism (*uccheda*).
Seeing that [Zhang San] was not there, Master Zhaogong said, "Last year, Zhang San was not non-existent. This refutes the view of non-existence.
If that is so, the next line says, "To demand the thing from its former state, yet it is not found in the present"—this certainly refutes the views held by worldly people.
Thus, worldly people would reckon that Zhang San was non-existent last year and existent this year. If that were the case...
Then Zhang San died last year, yet he has come back to life this year. Otherwise, from where would the people of the world have given rise to their views?
Since such views do not exist, for what reason did Master Sengzhao refute them when they have never existed until now?
If you claim that the latter phrase does not refute the view of "never having existed," then the former phrase’s determination that things "never have been non-existent" must likewise not be refuted.

There is no such thing as "non-existence. Furthermore, if Zhang San did not exist even in the past, there is no principle by which he could come back to life; thus, if he was non-existent then, he is non-existent now as well.
Yet you, Master Ren, claim that Master Zhao maintained that he was never non-existent in the past; this is equivalent to asserting that Zhang San exists in a place where he does not.
Therefore, to take "no-thing" as a "thing" means that the subsequent phrase has never existed even now; yet you further speak of "non-existence" regarding where Zhang San has no place to be.
This is thus to take "no-thing" as "no-thing. Not only is this shallow and vulgar, but it is also contradictory and deviant;
it is insufficient to serve as an assistant to Master Sengzhao and is instead sufficient only to increase Master Sengzhao's faults.
To the Venerable Anonymus (with his words attached):

For one who expounds the Dharma well, the priority lies in grasping the essential meaning rather than clinging to the literal words; it lies in skillful adaptation rather than rigid adherence to fixed rules.
The Tathāgata’s bequeathed teachings are like the Art of War by Sun Zi; for one who employs them effectively, the priority lies in responding to the immediate circumstances.
Spiritual transformation (*ṛddhi-vikurvaṇā*). If one stubbornly adheres to conventional laws without knowing how to adapt through change, few will not meet with failure.
Master Sengzhao’s exposition of the Dharma was itself a manifestation of spiritual transformation. How can it be challenged by using the doctrine of death and killing as a pretext?

As the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* states that all phenomena are impermanent while the Buddha-nature is permanent, the Sixth Patriarch, however, said that the Buddha-nature is impermanent and all phenomena are [permanent].
"Constant. How can one raise the objection that this is a fixed dharma?
Under the gate of the Patriarchs, people were never bound by real dharmas; this is merely one instance of administering medicine according to the illness.
It arises because when people hear the teachings of the Sūtras, they give rise to attachments based on the literal words, taking the Buddha-nature to be definitively constant. All...
It is established that all phenomena are impermanent. Yet the Patriarch turned this case upside down, saying: "Buddha-nature is impermanent; all phenomena are permanent. His intent was this:
if Buddha-nature were invariably and eternally permanent, from what would all phenomena arise? It is because Buddha-nature is impermanent that all phenomena are produced.
If all phenomena were fixedly impermanent, they would not be identical with true permanence; there would be something existing apart from true permanence.
This is the nature of things. However, the words of the Patriarchs were originally intended to shatter attachments.

There are those who, upon hearing this, immediately fixate on the Buddha-nature as being impermanent and all dharmas as being eternally constant; they thereby cause nirvana to become impermanent and saṃsāra to become eternal.
If birth and death were permanent, there would ultimately be no liberation. If nirvāṇa were impermanent, then after the Buddhas had realized it, they would return to undergo birth and death.
This would render the dharma of the Buddhas of the three periods—both for their own benefit and for the benefit of others—entirely false and deceptive.
How could any evil view be more extreme than this? The *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* says: "As long as the Dharma-eye has not been fully penetrated, one should not engage in such discrimination."
Whether the body of the Tathāgata is definitively permanent or impermanent can only be accepted through reverent faith.

If one were to say that the Tathāgata is definitively impermanent, one’s tongue would split and one would die to enter hell. A Bodhisattva who protects the Dharma would rather sacrifice their own life than say that the Buddha’s body is conditioned;
they must say that the Buddha’s body is an unconditioned dharma, definitively eternal, and incapable of change.
Indeed, the Buddha-body is the Dharma-body. The Dharma-body, Nirvana, and Buddha-nature—these three are merely different names for the same reality.
This is the Tathāgata’s final exertion, emptying his withered bowels to reveal the truth in its entirety. How could one then claim that the teaching of Nirvana is not yet fully realized?
Those who discourse on the doctrines must be cautious indeed! Nevertheless, the Zen of the Patriarchs is none other than our own Prajñā.
This is the essence of our school. Throughout the six hundred fascicles of the *Prajñāpāramitā*, not a single dharma—whether mundane or supramundane—is said to be real.

This is precisely what the Patriarchs meant when they said: "Do not seek the truth; simply cease all views. It is as they said: "I only wish that you empty away all that exists; be careful not to reify that which does not exist.
This is the "path of no-entrance" of the Zen school. Thus, the Sixth Patriarch pointed to Buddha-nature as being impermanent; this is the ancient...
The so-called discourse on the non-attainment of principle and the non-attainment of phenomena is entirely the purport of Prajñāpāramitā.
Therefore, within the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā*, such things as true thusness (*tathatā*), buddha-nature (*buddhadhātu*), bodhi, and nirvāṇa are all swept away. It even states:
"If there were a single dharma that transcended nirvāṇa, I would likewise declare it to be like a dream and like an illusion. This is for the bodhisattva who studies Prajñāpāramitā.
It must indeed be so. If it were not so, it would be insufficient to clarify *prajñā*.

For if it were otherwise, even if one were to discourse at length on *tathatā*, *buddhadhātu*, *bodhi*, and *nirvāṇa* for an entire lifetime, these would not transcend the realm of dreams and delusions;

how, then, could they suffice to reveal the true and eternal nature of *nirvāṇa*? This applies even to the *Śūraṅgama-sūtra*, the *Nirvāṇa-sūtra*, the *Śrīmālā-sūtra*, and the *Tathāgatagarbha-sūtra*.

The scriptures of the ultimate and final reality, such as those of the *Tathāgatagarbha* tradition, all teach that the Buddha-nature is truly permanent and unchanging, while all phenomena are adventitious, subject to arising and ceasing, and devoid of intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*). Since they lack intrinsic nature, they are not separate from the Truth.
Thus, the *Dharmabherī-sūtra* states: "The *Ākāśasama-sūtra* is of provisional meaning (*neyārtha*). This refers precisely to this point. Indeed, the *Sūtras* are [the teachings] of all Buddhas...

This is the Seal of the Dharma. Since ancient times, whenever a teacher of men has attained awakening, no matter how many thousands or tens of thousands of explanations they may offer, there has never been one that does not accord with the Sūtras.
This is what is meant by "the same script for writing and the same tracks for chariots. If it does not accord, it is either something different or heterodox. It is like a skilled general:

though their tactics may undergo a thousand transformations and ten thousand changes, there is never one that does not accord with the principles of military strategy. A questioner asked: "The Sixth Patriarch..."

Question: If it is said that the Buddha-nature is impermanent, with which sutra does this accord? Answer: The *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra* states: "That which is neither born nor extinguished is the meaning of impermanence.
The *Nirvāṇa-sūtra* also contains this same meaning, namely: "The afflictions and the Buddha-nature are originally present but now absent," and so forth.

Seeking this through principle (*li*), both principle and phenomena (*shi*) each possess the meanings of permanence and impermanence. As for principle, it is impermanent because it follows conditions, yet permanent because it is unchanging.
As for phenomena, they are impermanent because they manifest as characteristics, yet permanent because their essence is empty.

Thus, the words of the Sixth Patriarch regarding the meaning of permanence and impermanence naturally accord with the scriptural teachings. This demonstrates that when the words of the Sixth Patriarch are sought within the teachings, they are found therein.

There is evidence for this. When sought through principle, it is also consistent with principle; yet Master Zhao [Sengzhao] maintained that "past things do not transform" and that "natures each abide separately.
When sought through the teachings, there is no textual corroboration; when sought through principle, it is not yet fully consistent.
If there were a way to achieve consistency, I would certainly be willing to hear your instructions.
A Poem on the Words of Chan Master Kaizang of Mizaiguan (with an appended letter), which says:
"All within the borders of the realm are subjects of the King. Some stubbornly maintain that when Shun was the Son of Heaven, Gao Sou faced north to pay court to him.
A commentator explained this by saying: "Of the remaining people of Zhou, not a single one survived. This is...

Is it truly the case that no single person among the people was left behind? You have interpreted the *Śīkṣānanda* well; it is appropriate not to let the literal phrasing obstruct the underlying meaning.

As for Master Zhaor’s doctrine of non-transmigration, from my humble perspective, its primary tenet is simply that phenomena do not reach one another. It takes the abiding of each phenomenon in its own fundamental position as its core principle.
His citations of the *Prajñāpāramitā* sūtras and his claims regarding what existed in the past but is now absent, or what is neither extinguished nor arrives, [all support this view].

This is the gist of his argument. He employs a wide range of analogies, and his underlying intent appears to be as follows: I have privately observed that you refute [the opponent] by asserting that what existed in the past is now non-existent, thereby characterizing it as a view of permanence, nihilism, transience, or annihilation.

While this is indeed correct, I fear you may still not avoid the fault of making the blind Emperor Shun face north to pay court to his father, or the error of leaving not a single person remaining among the people of Zhou.
Furthermore, when the Tathāgata expounded the teachings, there were the Great and Small Vehicles, as well as the partial and...

The Perfect [Teaching] administers medicine according to the illness; from the outset, it has no fixed prescription. How could one possibly constrain it entirely with the principles of the perfect and sudden teachings of the *Avataṃsaka* and *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*?
Regarding the two meanings of "non-transmigration" in the *Pózhōng* (Refutation), the first is "emptiness of nature" and the second is "reality.

In my humble opinion, Master Zhaò’s "non-transmigration" refers precisely to the meaning of reality. His citations of the *Prajñāpāramitā* and other sūtras appear to be instances where he borrows their intent for his own purpose.
This is not his fundamental tenet. It cannot be so. What kind of person was Master Sengzhao? Why has he gone back to such extreme fragmentation compared to the past?
The Chan Master judges that Master Sengzhao’s doctrine of "non-transmigration" takes as its tenet that dharmas do not reach one another and that each dharma abides in its own original position.
One merely sees their words but has not yet examined their meaning in detail. Nevertheless, the Tathāgata, the Dharma King, possesses two kinds of dharma seals (dharmamudrā) that seal all phenomena:
first, the seal of dependent origination and cessation; second, the seal of true emptiness and the real mark (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*).
Since the time of the Tathāgata, whatever has been taught must correspond with these two seals to be considered the correct teaching. If it does not correspond with these two seals...

To respond [to this] would be a heterodox teaching. This indeed does not concede to any ordinary or holy being, whether ancient or modern. Furthermore, the first seal is also called the Seal of Impermanence:

all phenomena that arise through conditions must inevitably disperse and perish. If there were even a hair’s breadth of a thing that did not disperse and perish, then the Buddha would not have appeared in the world.
Thus, the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* says: "That which was originally non-existent now exists; that which was originally existent..."
Now, it is impossible for there to be dharmas that exist in all three periods of time. Furthermore, it is said: "All conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) are impermanent;
they are dharmas subject to arising and ceasing. The *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* states: "The conduct of all ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*) inevitably and swiftly returns to extinction.

All such passages speak of the cessation of the cause and the arising of the fruit, where the preceding thought-moment ceases and the succeeding thought-moment arises. This is not like Master Zhao’s [Sengzhao’s] view that "past things do not transform" or that "ancient causes do not cease."
The second seal refers to the Tathāgata’s sealing of all phenomena with the single seal of the true mark of emptiness (*śūnyatā-tattva-lakṣaṇa*).
There is not a single phenomenon that is not empty and quiescent. If there were even a hair's breadth of substantiality that was not empty, the Buddha would not have appeared in the world.
The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states: "The prior limit of form (*rūpa*) cannot be apprehended; its middle limit and its posterior limit likewise cannot be apprehended.

Form is itself emptiness (*śūnyatā*); all phenomena (*dharma*) are thus. The *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* states: "Departing from marks (*lakṣaṇa*) and extinguishing marks, they ultimately return to emptiness.
Yet these two seals are but a single seal. This is because all phenomena, being impermanent, lack intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*); and because they lack intrinsic nature, they are empty.
For this reason, when the youth of the Snowy Mountains heard the rākṣasa’s verse—“All conditioned phenomena are impermanent; they are of the nature of arising and ceasing”—he sighed and said:

“This is the meaning of emptiness in the Mahāyāna. It is only by means of essential impermanence that one attains empty stillness; it is only by means of essential empty stillness that one attains the complete reality of every single thing.
Now, Master Zhao [Sengzhao] maintains that although things existed in the past, they do not undergo transformation, and that although causes...
If things produce effects yet do not perish, and if they neither perish nor transform, this contradicts the seal of impermanence (*anityatā-dharmamudrā*).

Since it contradicts impermanence while claiming there is no perishing or transformation, then things must possess a fixed nature (*svabhāva*). If things possess a fixed nature, this runs counter to the Mahāyāna seal of emptiness (*śūnyatāmudrā*).
Having thus contradicted the emptiness of intrinsic nature (*prakṛti-śūnyatā*) while asserting that things are "truly non-transmigratory," this is no different from clinging to a mirage as real.
How does this differ from the fruit of a flower blooming in empty space? Now, as for what is called the true mark (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*):
the true mark of the past is no different from the true mark of the present, and the true mark of the present is no different from the true mark of the past.
The true mark of existing things is no different from the true mark of non-existing things, and the true mark of non-existing things is no different from the true mark of existing things.
This is the true mark (*dharmatā*). It is what is called the non-duality of existence and non-existence, and the suchness of past and present.

One who realizes this meaning finds that the single assembly on Vulture Peak is as vividly present as it is now. This is not like Master Sengzhao, who sought the objects of the past in the past and regarded them as existent, yet regarded them as non-existent in the present.
The Chan Master judged that Sengzhao’s [view of] "non-transmigration" was based on the idea that phenomena do not reach one another, and that each phenomenon abides in its own source.
Taking "position" as the primary tenet—if the Master’s words regarding the fruition are indeed so, would they not contradict the Dharma-seal of the Dharma-King?
However, regarding the principle that phenomena do not reach one another, there are two explanations based on the holy teachings, both of which do not exceed two kinds of Dharma-seals.

First is the principle of dependent origination and cessation; as a sutra states: "Conditioned phenomena are momentary in their destruction; therefore, there is no possibility of them migrating from this [state] to that."
Regarding other locations: this location is the preceding moment of thought, while the other location is the subsequent moment of thought.

Because the preceding moment ceases, it does not reach the subsequent moment. Nirvana is like a wax seal being pressed into clay. As the seal and the clay meet, the seal is destroyed and the impression is formed;

yet the wax seal itself does not remain unchanged within the clay. Herein, the destruction of the seal and the formation of the impression serve as a metaphor for the cessation of the cause and the arising of the fruit.

Furthermore, "not changing while in the mud" means that the cause does not persist into the fruit. This is because each preceding thought-moment ceases and thus does not reach the succeeding thought-moment.
It is not as Master Sengzhao claimed, that although things exist from the past they do not undergo transformation, or that although the cause produces the fruit, the cause itself is not extinguished.
Second is the meaning of the true mark of ultimate emptiness (*tathatā*). Because phenomena and their intrinsic nature (*dharmatā*) are empty, they do not reach one another.
This is not to say they do not reach; rather, reaching is itself non-reaching. The *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* says: "All phenomena have no activity, nor do they possess any substantial nature.
Therefore, all of them are mutually unaware of one another, like the waves of a mirage-water that do not touch one another. For this reason:
Because the object of the preceding thought is empty and devoid of intrinsic nature, it does not contact the succeeding thought; the same applies to the succeeding thought.

One who realizes this principle knows that water does not contact moisture, fire does not contact dryness, earth does not contact dust, and wind does not contact air. Dust-particle meets dust-particle without reaching one another;
moment meets moment without reaching one another. This is not like Master Sengzhao’s view that "the former thing is not extinguished" and its nature abides in the past.
It is not that it has not been so until now. Now, as for those who speak of the emptiness of nature (*prakṛti-śūnyatā*): if there is a nature, it is empty.

Thus, when things of the past existed in the past, their essential nature was already empty before the conditions had dispersed. How could one say that they were existent in the past and nonexistent in the present?

Furthermore, the holy teachings of the Tathāgata have endured for a thousand years; that the heterodox and evil doctrines of outsiders have been unable to corrupt or disrupt them is due to two [reasons].
The two seals of the Dharma (dharmamudrā) are well known by name; therefore, the holy teachings take names and phrases as their essence.
Indeed, these two seals of the Dharma cannot be altered even if a thousand Buddhas appear in the world.

How then can an ordinary person of the mundane realm dare to attempt to change the Dharma of the Dharma-King with the frivolous discursive arguments of the secular world? The Chan Master cites the poem: "Throughout all lands..."
"Those on the borders are all subjects of the King," yet it is possible that even Gao Yao was not a subject of Emperor Shun; one must not let the literal phrasing obscure the underlying intent.
Is it not the case that you take the Tathāgata’s holy words—that what is "originally existent" is now non-existent—to mean that everything is impermanent, shifting, and ceasing?

Yet you alone grant that the "originally existent, now non-existent" described by Master Zhaowang constitutes permanence and non-transience. If this were so, then [your interpretation of] the *Nirvāṇa*...
To claim that there is no basis for the Dharma of the three periods of time as spoken from the Golden Mouth [of the Buddha] is to produce a view that is utterly false and delusory.
It seems you take the frivolous discourses of worldly convention as your foundation, seeking thereby to subvert the Dharma-seal of the Dharma-King.
Now, the Dharma-seal of the Dharma-King cannot be altered by any of the thousand sages; how could it ever be destroyed by worldly talk? As for those who speak thus—
This is to destroy their own views. However, during the forty years that the Tathāgata preached the Dharma, there were certainly not no hidden or concealed teachings;
there were discourses of expedient means given according to the capacities of beings that remained unelucidated. At the very end, he fully revealed and opened them up, as it is said:
"While all rivers are winding and crooked, there are some that are not; while all women are flatterers and crooked, there are also [some who are not]."
Regarding those who are not deceitful or crooked: although one who kills their father or mother will inevitably fall into hell, there are also those who achieve the Path of the Sages.
This is because they kill the father of ignorance and the mother of craving. This is explained in detail in the *Nirvāṇa-sūtra*, which provides the full exposition for this point.

This is because [the Buddha] feared it would lead sentient beings into doubt and error. Now, when the Buddha says that what "existed originally is now non-existent," he necessarily means it is impermanent, subject to change and extinction;

I have never heard him allow for such a statement regarding something that is eternally abiding and immutable. The Buddha says that all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) perish in each moment (*kṣaṇa*);
I have never heard of an entity from the past remaining in the past without undergoing transformation. The Buddha says that the preceding aggregates (*skandha*) cease and the succeeding ones arise...

The effect arises while the cause has not yet ceased; I have never heard of such a thing. The Buddha taught that because the essence and function of all phenomena are empty, they do not cognize one another.
I have never heard it said that the natures of things each abide in a single moment and do not reach one another.
These are all conditions newly introduced outside the Dharma of the Dharma King. How can I follow them?

However, since Master Sengzhao has already cited the *Prajñāpāramitā* as the fundamental source [of his thought], yet claims it is not his own primary doctrine, this is once again the Venerable Sir contradicting Master Sengzhao himself.
Furthermore, how far apart could "emptiness of nature" (*prakṛti-śūnyatā*) and "true reality" (*bhūtārtha*) possibly be?
How could one who turns their back on emptiness of nature ever be able to realize true reality? To turn one's back on emptiness of nature while demanding true reality is precisely what is—

This means that one is stubbornly clinging to a flower in the sky while mistaking a mirage for reality. A Zen master must certainly hold that the nature of *prajñā* is emptiness (*śūnyatā*), whereas the nature of the *Lotus Sūtra* is abiding.

People know only that the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* clarifies the true mark (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*), yet they have never known that the six hundred fascicles of the *Prajñāpāramitā* speak exclusively of the true mark.

Would the profound meaning of the Sage’s teaching—that the true nature (*dharmatā*) is eternally abiding and immutable—have been allowed to sink into non-transformation due to this treatise?

With Master Zhaohui’s own brilliance, would he have willingly accepted such a conclusion? Furthermore, how could one know that the one who now offers this critique is not, in fact, Master Zhaohui himself?
